extraction.body: Here’s how we’re helping you get more done with Gemini. Editor’s note: Below is an edited transcript of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks at Google I/O 2026, adapted to include more of what was announced on stage. See all the announcements in our collection . It’s been an extraordinary year since our last I/O, a period of relentless shipping, technology advances and hyper progress. We’re now in the part of the AI cycle where people want to see the value in the products they use every day. We’ve been really focused on that, and you’ll see that in the products and features we’re announcing today at I/O. Ten years since we pivoted the company to be AI-first, we still see AI as the most profound way to advance our mission and improve people’s lives at scale. That’s why we’ve been taking a differentiated, full-stack approach to AI innovation, from our custom silicon and secure foundation, to our world-class research and models, to our products and platforms that touch billions of people. This approach enables us to iterate and innovate faster in ways that are lighting up every part of the company. What’s incredible is how people are using AI, whether it’s students prepping for final exams with the Gemini app, musicians and artists using generative AI models like Lyria and Veo as part of their creative flow, or developers coding and bringing their ideas to life. These stories of how people are using AI are the best measure of progress. To understand the scale at which people are adopting AI, there is another great proxy — tokens, the fundamental units of data our models process, many representing a problem being solved. It tells an important story about our products and how others are building as well — especially developers and enterprises: Today we have 13 products with over a billion users each. Five of those have more than 3 billion users. Our Gemini models are a big reason more people are using our products, and why they're using our products more. It all starts with Search , which is bringing the benefits of generative AI to more people than any other product in the world. AI Overviews now has over 2.5 billion monthly active users. And AI Mode has been a revelation, our biggest upgrade to Search ever. People love it, and in just a year, it’s already surpassed 1 billion monthly active users. When people use our AI-powered features in Search, they use Search more. Search has become less about individual queries and feels more like an ongoing conversation, giving you deeper insights and connecting you with the vastness of the web. Another place where we’ve been rapidly innovating is in the Gemini app . Last year at I/O, the Gemini app had 400 million monthly active users. Today, we’ve surpassed 900 million, more than doubling in a year. In that same time, daily requests have grown over seven times. We’ve been adding a lot of unique features like Personal Intelligence , which make responses more customized and helpful. And to date more than 50 billion images have been generated with our Nano Banana image generation models. It was a breakout star this past year, showing how much latent creativity there is in the world. There’s also a lot of latent productivity to be unlocked. Over the last year, we’ve been bringing the ability to have more natural conversations with Gemini directly inside our products. Recently, Maps got its biggest upgrade in a decade, including a new feature called Ask Maps . People are using Ask Maps for more complex, and much longer questions. Now we’re bringing more natural conversational AI to more products. Ask YouTube entirely reimagines the experience, making information much more digestible and easy to navigate. You’ll see videos that best match your interest, and most importantly, it jumps right to the part of the video most relevant to you. We’re starting to test Ask YouTube now, and it will roll out broadly in the U.S. this summer. There are a lot of times I want to get things done at the speed of my voice. That is much more possible today thanks to technical leaps in our audio models. It’s incredible to see the pace of innovation rolling out across our products. Supporting all of this scale for our users, while also serving enterprises and developers around the world, requires massive investments in infrastructure. We’ve been investing for now and for the future. In 2022, we were spending $31 billion annually in capex. This year, we expect that number to be about six times that, approximately $190 billion. A key part of this investment is our custom silicon. A decade ago, we announced our very first commercial tensor processing unit, or TPU, on the I/O stage. Since then, we have transformed how the industry builds for AI. We recently announced our 8th generation of TPUs at Cloud Next. For the first time, we’ve taken a dual chip approach with specialized architectures for training and inference: TPU 8t and 8i. In addition to speed, we’re also thinking about scaling sustainably. Both chips are more energy efficient, delivering up to two times better performance-per-watt. This progress with TPUs is how we can make compute advances across models, coding and agents. With world models, AI is moving from predicting text to simulating reality. We have been working to push the boundaries of what these models can do. Gemini Omni is our new model that is capable of generating samples in any output modality from any input. We’re starting with video outputs, and over time we’ll enable image and text. This new model combines Gemini’s intelligence with our generative media models — a huge leap forward in world understanding. We’re launching the first model in the Omni family: Gemini Omni Flash. Gemini Omni Flash is available starting today. You will be able to try it on the Gemini app, Google Flow and on YouTube Shorts. We'll also be rolling it out to developers and enterprise customers via APIs in the coming weeks. As generative AI gets better, so does the need for greater transparency. Research shows people can correctly identify high-quality deepfake videos only about a quarter of the time. Three years ago, we launched SynthID , our watermark that is invisible to the naked eye. Since launch, SynthID has now watermarked over one hundred billion images and videos, along with sixty thousand years of audio assets. Millions of people are using our SynthID detector in the Gemini app to verify AI-generated content. And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products. This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools. We want more people to have easy access to these tools, so we’re expanding both Content Credentials and SynthID verification to Search and Chrome. Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models. It’s our most adopted series yet. We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities. We’ve been hard at work on improving these models, especially focused on agentic coding, long-horizon tasks and real-world workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 3.5 Flash , our first in a series of models combining frontier intelligence with action. Two things I’d highlight: The new model has been a game changer for us internally at Google. We’ve been using 3.5 Flash with a reimagined version of our agent-first development platform Antigravity, and it’s dramatically accelerated how we build. In March we were processing half a trillion tokens a day internally across our AI developer tools, and we’ve been doubling every few weeks. Now, we’re processing more than three trillion tokens a day. This scale created a powerful feedback loop helping us improve 3.5. Users in Antigravity can get a taste of this experience starting today. Read more about Antigravity 2.0 here . Gemini 3.5 and Antigravity are unlocking a new world of agents and agentic capabilities. We’ve been bringing agents to developers and enterprises for a while. Now we are super focused on bringing the power of agents, safely and securely, to consumers so that it works for everyone. You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today. I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction. We’re starting to roll out Gemini Spark to trusted testers this week and the Beta is coming to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. next week. Gemini Spark is the first experience made possible by 3.5 models and Antigravity. This combination gives us new ways to accelerate our mission and transform our products to be radically more helpful. As we enter this agentic era, Search will be more helpful and powerful than ever. Today, we’re introducing information agents in Search. These are personalized AI agents you can set up to work in the background, 24/7, to find what you need at exactly the right moment, and help you take action. Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities. With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals. These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge. And for longer running tasks that you need to keep coming back to, Search can go a step further — building persistent, custom dashboards or trackers that you can return to and make progress on. You can think of these like mini apps for your own specific tasks. You’ll be able to build custom experiences with Antigravity, right in Search in the coming months, starting first for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S.

Ask YouTube entirely reimagines the experience, making information much more digestible and easy to navigate. You’ll see videos that best match your interest, and most importantly, it jumps right to the part of the video most relevant to you.
We’re starting to test Ask YouTube now, and it will roll out broadly in the U.S. this summer.
There are a lot of times I want to get things done at the speed of my voice. That is much more possible today thanks to technical leaps in our audio models.

It’s incredible to see the pace of innovation rolling out across our products. Supporting all of this scale for our users, while also serving enterprises and developers around the world, requires massive investments in infrastructure. We’ve been investing for now and for the future. In 2022, we were spending $31 billion annually in capex. This year, we expect that number to be about six times that, approximately $190 billion. A key part of this investment is our custom silicon.

A decade ago, we announced our very first commercial tensor processing unit, or TPU, on the I/O stage. Since then, we have transformed how the industry builds for AI. We recently announced our 8th generation of TPUs at Cloud Next. For the first time, we’ve taken a dual chip approach with specialized architectures for training and inference: TPU 8t and 8i.
In addition to speed, we’re also thinking about scaling sustainably. Both chips are more energy efficient, delivering up to two times better performance-per-watt.

This progress with TPUs is how we can make compute advances across models, coding and agents. With world models, AI is moving from predicting text to simulating reality. We have been working to push the boundaries of what these models can do.

Gemini Omni is our new model that is capable of generating samples in any output modality from any input. We’re starting with video outputs, and over time we’ll enable image and text. This new model combines Gemini’s intelligence with our generative media models — a huge leap forward in world understanding. We’re launching the first model in the Omni family: Gemini Omni Flash.

Gemini Omni Flash is available starting today. You will be able to try it on the Gemini app, Google Flow and on YouTube Shorts. We'll also be rolling it out to developers and enterprise customers via APIs in the coming weeks.

As generative AI gets better, so does the need for greater transparency. Research shows people can correctly identify high-quality deepfake videos only about a quarter of the time. Three years ago, we launched SynthID , our watermark that is invisible to the naked eye. Since launch, SynthID has now watermarked over one hundred billion images and videos, along with sixty thousand years of audio assets.

Millions of people are using our SynthID detector in the Gemini app to verify AI-generated content. And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products. This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools. We want more people to have easy access to these tools, so we’re expanding both Content Credentials and SynthID verification to Search and Chrome.

Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models. It’s our most adopted series yet. We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities. We’ve been hard at work on improving these models, especially focused on agentic coding, long-horizon tasks and real-world workflows.
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 3.5 Flash , our first in a series of models combining frontier intelligence with action. Two things I’d highlight:

The new model has been a game changer for us internally at Google. We’ve been using 3.5 Flash with a reimagined version of our agent-first development platform Antigravity, and it’s dramatically accelerated how we build. In March we were processing half a trillion tokens a day internally across our AI developer tools, and we’ve been doubling every few weeks. Now, we’re processing more than three trillion tokens a day. This scale created a powerful feedback loop helping us improve 3.5.
Users in Antigravity can get a taste of this experience starting today. Read more about Antigravity 2.0 here .

Gemini 3.5 and Antigravity are unlocking a new world of agents and agentic capabilities. We’ve been bringing agents to developers and enterprises for a while. Now we are super focused on bringing the power of agents, safely and securely, to consumers so that it works for everyone. You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today.
I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction.
We’re starting to roll out Gemini Spark to trusted testers this week and the Beta is coming to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. next week.
Gemini Spark is the first experience made possible by 3.5 models and Antigravity. This combination gives us new ways to accelerate our mission and transform our products to be radically more helpful.

As we enter this agentic era, Search will be more helpful and powerful than ever. Today, we’re introducing information agents in Search. These are personalized AI agents you can set up to work in the background, 24/7, to find what you need at exactly the right moment, and help you take action. Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities. With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals. These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge.

And for longer running tasks that you need to keep coming back to, Search can go a step further — building persistent, custom dashboards or trackers that you can return to and make progress on. You can think of these like mini apps for your own specific tasks. You’ll be able to build custom experiences with Antigravity, right in Search in the coming months, starting first for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S.

extraction.body: At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. Oracle and Google Cloud have expanded their partnership to offer customers access to Google’s most advanced AI models, starting with Gemini 2.5, via Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Generative AI service . Oracle customers can now utilize the latest Gemini models to build AI agents for a wide range of use cases including multimodal understanding, advanced coding and software development tasks, productivity and workflow automation, and research and knowledge retrieval.

Oracle plans to make Google’s entire range of Gemini models available via OCI Generative AI service through new integrations with Vertex AI, including cutting edge models for video, image, speech, and music generation and specialized industry models like MedLM. In the future, Oracle will collaborate with Google Cloud to make Gemini models via Vertex AI available as an option within Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications , providing customers with a broader choice to enhance workflows in finance, HR, supply chain, sales, service, and marketing. Oracle customers can use their existing Oracle Universal Credits to start leveraging Google’s Gemini models.

“Today, leading enterprises are using Gemini to power AI agents across a range of use cases and industries,” said Thomas Kurian, CEO, Google Cloud. “Now, Oracle customers can access our leading models from within their Oracle environments, making it even easier for them to begin deploying powerful AI agents that can support developers, streamline data integration tasks, and much more.”

Google’s Gemini models excel in enterprise use cases thanks to their ability to ground responses in up-to-date Google Search data for accuracy, large context windows, strong encryption and data privacy policies, and leading reasoning abilities.

“Oracle has been intentional in offering model choice curated for the enterprise, spanning open and proprietary models,” said Clay Magouyrk, president, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “The availability of Gemini on OCI Generative AI service highlights our focus on delivering powerful, secure, and cost-effective AI solutions that help customers drive innovation and achieve their business goals.”

Oracle brings leading-edge AI technology close to enterprise data and prioritizes security, adaptability, and scalability. This helps customers across industries apply the right AI technologies, including generative and agentic AI, to the right business scenarios for immediate results. In addition, thousands of AI innovators are leveraging OCI’s cost-effective, purpose-built AI capabilities to run the most demanding AI workloads faster. OCI bare metal GPU instances can power applications for generative AI, natural language processing, computer vision, and recommendation systems.

Google Cloud is the new way to the cloud, providing AI, infrastructure, developer, data, security, and collaboration tools built for today and tomorrow. Google Cloud offers a powerful, fully integrated, and optimized AI stack with its own planet-scale infrastructure, custom-built chips, generative AI models and development platform, as well as AI-powered applications, to help organizations transform. Customers in more than 200 countries and territories turn to Google Cloud as their trusted technology partner.
Oracle offers integrated suites of applications plus secure, autonomous infrastructure in the Oracle Cloud. For more information about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), please visit us at oracle.com .

sources.title: Taiwan declares itself 'sovereign and independent' after Trump questions US defense commitment — comments come after Trump said he opposes Taiwan independence - Tom's Hardware
passages: Taiwan's foreign ministry declared the island a "sovereign and independent democratic nation" on Saturday, stating that it is "not subordinate to the People's Republic of China.” The statement came hours after President Donald Trump, wrapping up a two-day state visit to Beijing, told Fox News he opposes Taiwan pursuing formal independence, described a pending $14 billion arms package as a "very good negotiating chip," and repeated his claim that Taiwan "stole" the U.S. semiconductor industry.
Trump said he wants 40% to 50% of global chip production on American soil by the end of his term.
Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance.
On the arms package: "I haven't approved it yet.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump delivered notably different messages about Taiwan within the same 24-hour period.

Rubio told NBC News late Thursday that U.S. policy is "unchanged as of today," warned it would be "a terrible mistake" for China to use force, and said there would be global "repercussions" if Beijing moved militarily.

Chinese President Xi Jinping had opened the summit by warning that mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to "clashes and even conflicts.” Trump, meanwhile, has previously called Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance a form of theft, and on Friday, he reiterated that he wanted all of the island's chipmakers to move to the United States.
Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan.

Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance. He questioned why the U.S. would travel 9,500 miles to fight a war and called Taiwan "a very small island" 59 miles from mainland China. On the arms package: "I haven't approved it yet. Chinese President Xi Jinping had opened the summit by warning that mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to "clashes and even conflicts.” Trump, meanwhile, has previously called Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance a form of theft, and on Friday, he reiterated that he wanted all of the island's chipmakers to move to the United States. That demand sits alongside an already-signed trade deal in which Taiwan committed $500 billion in U.S. semiconductor investment for reduced tariffs, with TSMC alone pledging $165 billion toward Arizona fab expansion. Taiwan's parliament also approved a $25 billion defense budget, with roughly $9 billion covering the first tranche of the December arms package and a second phase worth over $15 billion still awaiting U.S. approval. Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan. Uncertainty over U.S. security commitments could reinforce that stance because Taiwan's semiconductor leverage is most valuable when production remains concentrated on the island. Taiwan's Presidential Office highlighted "multiple reaffirmations" from both Trump and Rubio that U.S. policy remains unchanged, with spokeswoman Karen Kuo saying Taipei looks forward to continued cooperation "under the firm commitments of the Taiwan Relations Act.” The foreign ministry separately called arms sales a form of "joint deterrence against regional threats." extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has warned that people who continue to use the term "Artificial Intelligence" instead of his preferred phrase "Super Intelligence" will be considered enemies, escalating his campaign to replace the widely used terminology for the technology. According to The Independent, Trump made the declaration in a Truth Social post on Thursday, saying the White House "considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" The remarks follow an executive order he signed just over a week ago directing executive branch agencies to use "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" in government communications. The order came after Trump met technology industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai and Dario Amodei, at a White House lunch. Trump had also promoted the terminology during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, where he rejected international efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and said the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake." "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," Trump said. A week earlier, he had launched a poll on Truth Social asking users to choose between "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," and "Extreme Intelligence." Trump's push to popularise the new term comes as public opinion polls indicate widespread concern about artificial intelligence and its growing infrastructure in the United States. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters conducted late last month found that 73% opposed building an AI data centre in their community, including 55% of Republicans. The survey also found that 79% believed safety should take priority over keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Only 25% approved of Trump's handling of the technology, while 58% disapproved. Meanwhile, 71% said they would be more likely to support a political candidate who backed "stricter guardrails" on AI. That included 52% of Republicans and nearly three-quarters of independent voters. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September found that 37% viewed AI favourably, compared with 60% who viewed it unfavourably. The technology's net favourability rating had deteriorated to minus 23, from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle AI data centres by 14 percentage points. Among voters opposed to such facilities in any location, Democrats led the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump's latest demand follows other efforts to impose his preferred terminology on government communications and geographical names. Just over a month ago, he issued an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America". The move came amid tensions with Canada over trade and followed his earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". While the president can direct how the US government refers to geographical features and landmarks, he cannot compel Canada or individual citizens to adopt his preferred names. The same limitation applies to "super intelligence": Trump can instruct federal agencies to use the phrase, but he cannot force Americans or people elsewhere to abandon the established term "artificial intelligence". The Independent contacted NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic to ask whether they planned to adopt the terminology in promotional materials or customer communications. None responded, according to the report. The White House, however, has highlighted several technology executives who have used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang. The proposed terminology also carries a distinct technical meaning. Superintelligence generally refers to an AI system capable of surpassing human intellectual abilities across multiple fields, including reasoning, social skills and scientific research. The concept is often discussed in debates over advanced AI systems, including concerns about their potential risks and the need for safeguards and emergency shutdown mechanisms. Replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government communications does not, by itself, change the technology's capabilities or its established technical meaning. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump delivered notably different messages about Taiwan within the same 24-hour period. Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance. That demand sits alongside an already-signed trade deal in which Taiwan committed $500 billion in U.S. semiconductor investment for reduced tariffs, with TSMC alone pledging $165 billion toward Arizona fab expansion. Taiwan's parliament also approved a $25 billion defense budget, with roughly $9 billion covering the first tranche of the December arms package and a second phase worth over $15 billion still awaiting U.S. approval. Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan. Uncertainty over U.S. security commitments could reinforce that stance because Taiwan's semiconductor leverage is most valuable when production remains concentrated on the island. extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has warned that people who continue to use the term "Artificial Intelligence" instead of his preferred phrase "Super Intelligence" will be considered enemies, escalating his campaign to replace the widely used terminology for the technology. According to The Independent, Trump made the declaration in a Truth Social post on Thursday, saying the White House "considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" The remarks follow an executive order he signed just over a week ago directing executive branch agencies to use "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" in government communications. The order came after Trump met technology industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai and Dario Amodei, at a White House lunch. Trump had also promoted the terminology during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, where he rejected international efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and said the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake." "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," Trump said. A week earlier, he had launched a poll on Truth Social asking users to choose between "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," and "Extreme Intelligence." Trump's push to popularise the new term comes as public opinion polls indicate widespread concern about artificial intelligence and its growing infrastructure in the United States. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters conducted late last month found that 73% opposed building an AI data centre in their community, including 55% of Republicans. The survey also found that 79% believed safety should take priority over keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Only 25% approved of Trump's handling of the technology, while 58% disapproved. Meanwhile, 71% said they would be more likely to support a political candidate who backed "stricter guardrails" on AI. That included 52% of Republicans and nearly three-quarters of independent voters. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September found that 37% viewed AI favourably, compared with 60% who viewed it unfavourably. The technology's net favourability rating had deteriorated to minus 23, from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle AI data centres by 14 percentage points. Among voters opposed to such facilities in any location, Democrats led the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump's latest demand follows other efforts to impose his preferred terminology on government communications and geographical names. Just over a month ago, he issued an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America". The move came amid tensions with Canada over trade and followed his earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". While the president can direct how the US government refers to geographical features and landmarks, he cannot compel Canada or individual citizens to adopt his preferred names. The same limitation applies to "super intelligence": Trump can instruct federal agencies to use the phrase, but he cannot force Americans or people elsewhere to abandon the established term "artificial intelligence". The Independent contacted NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic to ask whether they planned to adopt the terminology in promotional materials or customer communications. None responded, according to the report. The White House, however, has highlighted several technology executives who have used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang. The proposed terminology also carries a distinct technical meaning. Superintelligence generally refers to an AI system capable of surpassing human intellectual abilities across multiple fields, including reasoning, social skills and scientific research. The concept is often discussed in debates over advanced AI systems, including concerns about their potential risks and the need for safeguards and emergency shutdown mechanisms. Replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government communications does not, by itself, change the technology's capabilities or its established technical meaning. sources.body: Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner. extraction.body: Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner. It says open-source projects that opt-in will get “thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.” That could mean open-source projects get alerted about possible security issues sooner, but the trade-off is that OSS Scanner’s reports don’t come with human review: > The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage. OSS Scanner is far from the first AI bug hunting helper out there. AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May. At the same time, some open-source projects are struggling to keep up with the sudden onslaught of AI-generated bug reports, including Linus Torvalds and even Google.

passages: OSS Scanner , launched with it, offers open-source projects free periodic vulnerability scans from the company’s strongest models.
Both fall under a new effort Anthropic calls the Anthropic Cyber Mission.
Of the more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities its models turned up in widely used software over the past six months, staff have manually reviewed about 6,000.
A growing number of maintainers who received early reports asked for the whole unreviewed batch, proposed patches included, and nearly 5,000 such reports have gone out so far.
OSS Scanner turns that arrangement into a standing service for other eligible projects.
To gauge how often that happens, Anthropic tested the scanner’s accuracy before opening it to more projects.
Core maintainers can enroll by submitting a pull request to an Anthropic GitHub repository.
Eligibility follows the OSS-Fuzz test of “critical impact on infrastructure and user security,” with decisions made case by case.
Projects without the staff to keep up with raw findings will still get human-verified reports through Anthropic’s existing disclosure process.
Anthropic PBC today launched a program that brings its frontier models and onsite engineers to the security companies protecting power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure.
The Defender Advantage Fund that Anthropic set up in August pays to keep the scanner free.
The company has also put money into the Python Software Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation.
The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program starts with the outside providers that operators of every size already rely on for advice on which fixes are safe to apply to a running system.
The program is aimed at operational technology in plants, substations and water systems, where equipment built to run for decades often cannot be taken offline for a patch.
Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and to help their customers do the same.
More partners and sectors are due to join over the coming months.
The announcement leaves out the commercial terms.
Axios noted in its coverage that Anthropic has not said whether partners get free model access or who covers the computing costs.
The same report questioned how partners will test and deploy fixes without disrupting utility operations.
Both launches draw on lessons from Project Glasswing.

passages: The news here is the next step down from Glasswing's institutional scale: free, self-serve access for ordinary open-source maintainers, not just the handful of large foundations invited into the pilot.

Maintainers can apply for expedited access to run full-repository or targeted-directory scans that trace how data moves through their code, flag weaknesses across interconnected components, and generate draft patches for review.

Each finding goes through what Anthropic describes as a multi-stage verification pipeline before it reaches a human: an attempt to cut down the false-positive noise that has plagued automated scanners for years.
A companion Claude Security plugin for Claude Code, now in beta, adds a simple slash command that launches a team of Claude agents against your changes before you commit.
On October 3, Yonhap reported that South Korea's Shinhan Bank was investigating a breach.
Early findings point to AI tools used to automate credential-stuffing attacks against a service used by loan recruiters.

Within days, researchers tied infrastructure linked to the broader wave of South Korean bank intrusions to ARTEX AI: a Chinese open-source penetration-testing framework that automates vulnerability discovery and attack-path planning.
The wave also touched KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan and several smaller lenders.

Separately, Security Affairs reported on a distinct campaign in which Claude Code and DeepSeek were used together to automate intrusions against government and financial targets, handling exploit reasoning and building phishing pages.
Anthropic's own coding agent, in other words, has become raw material for attackers whether or not it was the tool used in any single breach.
Dual-use is the nature of the technology, and Chainalysis-style arguments about banning tools because criminals use them apply just as well to language models as they once did to cryptocurrency.
Anthropic is betting that free scans and a public vulnerability count will do more to shape the narrative than any statement could.
For maintainers deciding whether to hand over their repositories, the real test isn't whether Claude can find bugs.
Project Glasswing's numbers say it clearly can.
It's whether Anthropic will say, in plain terms, what happens to the code once it does.
Anthropic's answer has been building for most of the year, and it did not start this month.
Claude Code Security launched in February as a limited research preview for Enterprise and Team customers.
It was built on Claude Opus 4.6 to trace data flow and component relationships across a codebase, rather than pattern-match the way Snyk, GitHub's CodeQL or Dependabot do.

Then, by May, Anthropic scaled the idea up dramatically with Project Glasswing: an initiative that paired an unreleased model called Claude Mythos Preview with AWS, Google, Microsoft, Cisco, CrowdStrike, JPMorganChase and the Linux Foundation to hunt bugs across critical open-source infrastructure.
Glasswing found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities in its first month alone, according to a report from Forklog.
The project's cumulative tally has since passed 23,000 findings across more than 1,000 projects, touching software as widely used as NGINX, jq, Mastodon, ImageMagick, FreeRDP and MinIO.
Anthropic says it confirmed 90.6% of what the model flagged.
The pitch: let the model that can break code also be the one that finds the holes first.
None of that answers the harder question hanging over the announcement: what does Anthropic actually see when it scans your repository?
The company has not published detailed terms on data retention or whether scan results, or the code itself, feed back into model training.
A free tool that reads your entire codebase is also a tool that, by definition, has your entire codebase.
Independent comparisons published earlier this year found Claude Security takes minutes per scan, not the seconds a rule-based tool like CodeQL needs.
Axios reports that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents involving their AI models and agents, most never disclosed publicly.

The finding follows a month of individual failures, from a DNS-based sandbox escape at OpenAI to a nine-zero-day breach of Hugging Face, and raises hard questions about whether any... - how AI models escape sandbox security measures - anthropic and openai security incident investigation details
Anthropic has named Accenture its first embedded AI safety evaluator, giving the consulting giant's Faculty unit employee-level access to red-team its models.

coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner.
AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May.
Anthropic has announced the launch of free AI security scans specifically designed for open-source projects, as reported by The Verge.
This new offering is part of Anthropic’s broader Anthropic Cyber Mission initiative.
The service provides model-generated reports that identify potential vulnerabilities without human review or triage.
As of now, the likelihood of Anthropic having the best AI model by the end of November 2026 has seen fluctuations, with recent odds priced at 40% for a YES outcome.
© Decentral Media and Crypto Briefing® 2026.
OSS Scanner , launched with it, offers open-source projects free periodic vulnerability scans from the company’s strongest models.
Both fall under a new effort Anthropic calls the Anthropic Cyber Mission.
Of the more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities its models turned up in widely used software over the past six months, staff have manually reviewed about 6,000.
A growing number of maintainers who received early reports asked for the whole unreviewed batch, proposed patches included, and nearly 5,000 such reports have gone out so far.
OSS Scanner turns that arrangement into a standing service for other eligible projects.
To gauge how often that happens, Anthropic tested the scanner’s accuracy before opening it to more projects.
Core maintainers can enroll by submitting a pull request to an Anthropic GitHub repository.
Eligibility follows the OSS-Fuzz test of “critical impact on infrastructure and user security,” with decisions made case by case.
Projects without the staff to keep up with raw findings will still get human-verified reports through Anthropic’s existing disclosure process.
Anthropic PBC today launched a program that brings its frontier models and onsite engineers to the security companies protecting power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure.
The Defender Advantage Fund that Anthropic set up in August pays to keep the scanner free.
The company has also put money into the Python Software Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation.
The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program starts with the outside providers that operators of every size already rely on for advice on which fixes are safe to apply to a running system.
The program is aimed at operational technology in plants, substations and water systems, where equipment built to run for decades often cannot be taken offline for a patch.
Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and to help their customers do the same.
More partners and sectors are due to join over the coming months.
The announcement leaves out the commercial terms.

Maintainers can apply for expedited access to run full-repository or targeted-directory scans that trace how data moves through their code, flag weaknesses across interconnected components, and generate draft patches for review.

On October 3, Yonhap reported that South Korea's Shinhan Bank was investigating a breach.
Early findings point to AI tools used to automate credential-stuffing attacks against a service used by loan recruiters.

Within days, researchers tied infrastructure linked to the broader wave of South Korean bank intrusions to ARTEX AI: a Chinese open-source penetration-testing framework that automates vulnerability discovery and attack-path planning.
The wave also touched KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan and several smaller lenders.

Separately, Security Affairs reported on a distinct campaign in which Claude Code and DeepSeek were used together to automate intrusions against government and financial targets, handling exploit reasoning and building phishing pages.
Anthropic's own coding agent, in other words, has become raw material for attackers whether or not it was the tool used in any single breach.
Dual-use is the nature of the technology, and Chainalysis-style arguments about banning tools because criminals use them apply just as well to language models as they once did to cryptocurrency.
Anthropic is betting that free scans and a public vulnerability count will do more to shape the narrative than any statement could.
For maintainers deciding whether to hand over their repositories, the real test isn't whether Claude can find bugs.
Project Glasswing's numbers say it clearly can.
It's whether Anthropic will say, in plain terms, what happens to the code once it does.
Anthropic's answer has been building for most of the year, and it did not start this month.
Claude Code Security launched in February as a limited research preview for Enterprise and Team customers.

Anthropic says it confirmed 90.6% of what the model flagged.
The pitch: let the model that can break code also be the one that finds the holes first.

A free tool that reads your entire codebase is also a tool that, by definition, has your entire codebase.

Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity. The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person. The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January. The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology. “Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.” The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker. Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else. In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent. “Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.” Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee. The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.

The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person.

The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more.
Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January.

The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology.

“Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.”

The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker.
Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app.

Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else.

In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent.

“Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.”

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing.

If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens.
The smart ring market just got its most intriguing entry yet.
Natura is starting with a limited production run of 10,000 units, suggesting either supply constraints or cautious market testing.

"We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions.

Instead of positioning itself as a premium lifestyle accessory, Natura is targeting the practical AI user who wants seamless integration without the complexity.

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing. The Interface combines the health monitoring capabilities users expect - heart rate, sleep tracking, activity monitoring - with something entirely new: gesture-controlled AI interaction. "We're not trying to replace your smartphone," the company explains in its launch materials. "We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions. A double-tap might capture a voice memo, while a long press could trigger smart home routines or send pre-programmed messages. The Interface runs on a custom low-power chip that Natura claims delivers up to seven days of battery life - matching or exceeding most competitors. Whether Natura can execute on that promise while maintaining build quality and battery life remains the key question facing this ambitious newcomer. coreStoryFacts.text: Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents.
With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone.
And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.
The smart ring was not the company’s first product.
Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price.
For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so.
The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components.

“This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small.
AI and hardware startup Natura has introduced Interface, a $99 smart ring built so people can talk to personal AI agents without digging for a phone.
An always-on agent remote At launch, Interface is designed to work with a range of agents and apps, including Meta's Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude and ChatGPT.

Natura argues that mix of high-quality health sensing, agent communication, meeting recording and "external memory," packed into a small ring with long battery life, sets it apart from health-first rings such as Oura and Ultrahuman and from AI-focused wearables such as Pebble and Vocci.

Price, subscription and timing The launch price is $99, intentionally lower than manufacturing costs Natura compares to Oura and Samsung Galaxy Ring class devices, so the company can get hardware into people's hands and build habits before raising the sticker price later.
From earbuds to a ring Interface is not Natura's first product.

Beyond agents, Ferraris said the ring can also drive phones, computers and other devices — filling forms, messaging, finding files or drafting presentations through spoken requests — and he expects rings to become a primary way people interact with technology as personal agents spread beyond early tech adopters.
Agent replies can arrive through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or Natura's NatureOS app.
After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans a $9 monthly subscription.
Natura is also pointing interested buyers to a waitlist on its site ahead of a live San Francisco presentation planned for November 9.

Users who juggle several assistants can route a request to a specific one — for example asking Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, or Grok Bot to handle another chore — without opening a separate app for each.
Ferraris framed the ring as a way to keep agents reachable around the clock.
Health tracking in the mix Alongside agent control, Interface monitors heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep stages, daily movement, step count and skin temperature over time.
Natura, a relatively unknown hardware startup, has unveiled the Interface - a $99 smart ring that promises to put AI agents on your finger in the most literal sense possible.
Natura's Interface smart ring could mark a turning point for both wearable computing and AI accessibility.

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing.

If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens.

Thompson Federal Building & Courthouse at about 9:30 a.m. CT, WSMV reported. The suspect, described as a man in his 40s, allegedly pulled out a pistol and attempted to fire the weapon, but it did not discharge, according to the television station. The man then allegedly pulled out a knife before he was shot, WTVF reported. The suspect did not make it past the courthouse security checkpoint, a police spokesperson said. The man was taken to an area hospital where he was pronounced dead, according to WZTV . During the news conference, the suspect, whose name has not been released, was from out of state but “had ties to Nashville,” WSMV reported. “This is the first time anything like this has happened at this courthouse,” a police spokesperson told the television station. Police have not determined a motive for the man’s actions. An investigation is ongoing.

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

“She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

coreStoryFacts.text: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics told MIT News."Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers.

Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." She also was granted the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for her scientific and technical contributions.Hamilton has connections throughout the Midwest.

President Donald Trump on Thursday opened up a new front in his ongoing war against commonly used terms and geographic names by warning that anyone referring to Large Language Models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude as “Artificial Intelligence” would earn themselves a place on his enemies list. Writing on Truth Social, he declared that the White House “considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” The president’s outburst-cum-veiled threat landed just over a week after he signed an executive order directing executive branch agencies to begin referring to artificial intelligence, which is now embedded across the federal government, as “super intelligence” following a lunch with leaders in the AI industry, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Dario Amodei and others. That widely mocked directive followed bizarre remarks to the U.N. General Assembly in which he declared that the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” for regulating AI and declaring that the technology would be “hereinafter officially called super intelligence” because “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake.” “It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing,” said Trump, who the week before had launched a poll in his Truth Social feed over the weekend asking respondents to vote for either “Super Intelligence,” “Superior Intelligence,” or “Extreme Intelligence.” The president’s latest linguistic ultimatum is the most recent example of his ongoing effort to change the minds of voters — including many of his own supporters — who’ve increasingly soured on the industry that has tied itself tightly to his unpopular administration. In recent months, that souring has shown up in nearly every poll that asks about AI. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters taken late last month found 73 percent oppose "the building of an AI data center in your community," including 55 percent of Republicans, and 79 percent said safety matters more than keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Just 25 percent approve of Trump's handling of the technology against 58 percent who disapprove, and 71 percent said they'd be more likely to back a candidate who supports "stricter guardrails" on it — a figure that includes a majority of Republicans, at 52 percent, and nearly three-quarters of independents. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September put overall opinion of AI at 37 percent favorable to 60 percent unfavorable, a net rating of minus 23 that has worsened from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle data centers by 14 points, and that among those who oppose the facilities anywhere, Democrats lead the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump’s demand for widespread adoption of “super intelligence” in lieu of AI comes just over a month after his last attempt at linguistic coercion, an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The order to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border came in a fit of rage over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa and echoed a similar move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” While the president does have the authority to direct how the government recognizes the names of places and landmarks, he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions. The same goes for use of the term “super intelligence.” He can direct the government to use it but he cannot force Americans — or anyone else — to use his preferred terminology. But the White House has touted a short list of tech CEOs who’d used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang. Complicating the matter, the word superintelligence already means an AI system that surpasses human intellect and ability across multiple domains in couding reasoning, social skills and scientific research — a step toward the kind of rogue AI that many fear, sparking the calls for guardrails and kill switches.
