extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

passages: That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969.
As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen.
The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing.
Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening.
Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility.
The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing.
A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software.
Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends.
The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash.
Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission.
Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously.
Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.”
The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015.

In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight.
Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term “software engineering” and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90.

A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the “Women of NASA” set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement.
She was the first programmer hired, and the first woman, working on six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972.
At the time, binary code was stored using copper wires wound around cores.
A “1” was a wire passing through a core, and a “0” was a wire bypassing the core.
New England textile workers were hired to weave them together into long ropes, earning Hamilton the moniker “rope mother,” since she was responsible for those ropes.
After the Apollo program ended, the Instrumentation Lab became the independent Draper Laboratory.
Hamilton worked there until 1976, when she founded Higher Order Software, based on her work on error prevention and fault tolerance.
In 1985, she left the company to found Hamilton Technologies.

extraction.body: Hamilton also coined the term “software engineering” and founded two successful software companies. Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term “software engineering” and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the “Women of NASA” set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.” Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics. She ended up working for Edward Lorenz, the MIT mathematician who set out to construct a mathematical model of the weather using a set of differential equations representing changes in temperature, pressure, wind velocity, and the like. You’ve probably heard the famous story of how Lorenz kept a continuous simulation running on his LGP-30 computer, and of that fateful 1961 day when he realized that even small differences in starting values could lead to very different outcomes—a sensitivity to initial conditions that is a hallmark of chaos theory, along with strange attractors. You might not have known that it was Hamilton who was responsible for programming the LGP-30. Computers were still a novelty at the time, and neither Lorenz nor Hamilton had any programming knowledge; they taught themselves. Per a 2019 Quanta article , Lorenz was amused by her unusual methods: For instance, she once bypassed the “clunky debugging process” by rolling the paper tape down the hallway and editing the binary code by hand with a pencil. “I’d poke holes for ones, and I’d cover up with Scotch tape the others,” she recalled. Hamilton moved to another project in 1961, but not before training her replacement: a recent math graduate from Mount Holyoke named Ellen Fetter. Lorenz acknowledged the contributions of both women in his papers. In 1961, Hamilton moved to the SAGE project at MIT, writing software for a prototype XD-1 computer to aid the US Air Force in searching for possible enemy aircraft. Her first challenge: deciphering a program nobody had managed to get to work, perhaps because the author’s notes were written in Latin and Greek. Hamilton succeeded, noting with amusement that the program even printed out its answers in Greek and Latin. It was during this period that she became interested in the issue of software reliability. By 1965, Hamilton was all set to go to graduate school as planned when her husband spotted a newspaper ad saying that MIT’s Instrumentation Lab needed people to develop onboard guidance computer software for NASA’s Apollo program. She was the first programmer hired, and the first woman, working on six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972. At the time, binary code was stored using copper wires wound around cores. A “1” was a wire passing through a core, and a “0” was a wire bypassing the core. New England textile workers were hired to weave them together into long ropes, earning Hamilton the moniker “rope mother,” since she was responsible for those ropes. Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends. The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash. Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission. Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously. Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish. Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.” By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Hamilton had the idea to incorporate a failsafe into the system software’s “priority display” interface routines, should the onboard guidance computer become overloaded with more tasks than it could handle in real time. That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969. As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen. The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing. Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening. Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility. As Hamilton herself later recalled in a 1971 letter : The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing. It then sent out an alarm, which meant to the astronaut, “I’m overloaded with more tasks than I should be doing at this time and I’m going to keep only the more important tasks”; i.e., the ones needed for landing … Actually, the computer was programmed to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software. The software’s action, in this case, was to eliminate lower priority tasks and re-establish the more important ones … If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful Moon landing it was. The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015. In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight. After the Apollo program ended, the Instrumentation Lab became the independent Draper Laboratory. Hamilton worked there until 1976, when she founded Higher Order Software, based on her work on error prevention and fault tolerance. In 1985, she left the company to found Hamilton Technologies. Its main product is the Universal Systems Language (USL) for developing complex software systems that prioritized error prevention and defensive programming. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great-grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the “Women of NASA” set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.”

Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics.

She ended up working for Edward Lorenz, the MIT mathematician who set out to construct a mathematical model of the weather using a set of differential equations representing changes in temperature, pressure, wind velocity, and the like. You’ve probably heard the famous story of how Lorenz kept a continuous simulation running on his LGP-30 computer, and of that fateful 1961 day when he realized that even small differences in starting values could lead to very different outcomes—a sensitivity to initial conditions that is a hallmark of chaos theory, along with strange attractors. You might not have known that it was Hamilton who was responsible for programming the LGP-30.

Computers were still a novelty at the time, and neither Lorenz nor Hamilton had any programming knowledge; they taught themselves. Per a 2019 Quanta article , Lorenz was amused by her unusual methods: For instance, she once bypassed the “clunky debugging process” by rolling the paper tape down the hallway and editing the binary code by hand with a pencil. “I’d poke holes for ones, and I’d cover up with Scotch tape the others,” she recalled. Hamilton moved to another project in 1961, but not before training her replacement: a recent math graduate from Mount Holyoke named Ellen Fetter. Lorenz acknowledged the contributions of both women in his papers.

In 1961, Hamilton moved to the SAGE project at MIT, writing software for a prototype XD-1 computer to aid the US Air Force in searching for possible enemy aircraft. Her first challenge: deciphering a program nobody had managed to get to work, perhaps because the author’s notes were written in Latin and Greek. Hamilton succeeded, noting with amusement that the program even printed out its answers in Greek and Latin. It was during this period that she became interested in the issue of software reliability.

By 1965, Hamilton was all set to go to graduate school as planned when her husband spotted a newspaper ad saying that MIT’s Instrumentation Lab needed people to develop onboard guidance computer software for NASA’s Apollo program. She was the first programmer hired, and the first woman, working on six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972. At the time, binary code was stored using copper wires wound around cores. A “1” was a wire passing through a core, and a “0” was a wire bypassing the core. New England textile workers were hired to weave them together into long ropes, earning Hamilton the moniker “rope mother,” since she was responsible for those ropes.

Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends. The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash. Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission. Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously. Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish. Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.”

By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Hamilton had the idea to incorporate a failsafe into the system software’s “priority display” interface routines, should the onboard guidance computer become overloaded with more tasks than it could handle in real time.

That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969. As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen. The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing. Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening. Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility.
As Hamilton herself later recalled in a 1971 letter :

The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing. It then sent out an alarm, which meant to the astronaut, “I’m overloaded with more tasks than I should be doing at this time and I’m going to keep only the more important tasks”; i.e., the ones needed for landing … Actually, the computer was programmed to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software. The software’s action, in this case, was to eliminate lower priority tasks and re-establish the more important ones … If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful Moon landing it was.

The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015. In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight.

After the Apollo program ended, the Instrumentation Lab became the independent Draper Laboratory. Hamilton worked there until 1976, when she founded Higher Order Software, based on her work on error prevention and fault tolerance. In 1985, she left the company to found Hamilton Technologies. Its main product is the Universal Systems Language (USL) for developing complex software systems that prioritized error prevention and defensive programming.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great-grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn.

The woman who sent men to the moon with a massive pile of software would never have become a programmer by a hair's breadth . But for her husband's tiresome career plans. What happened. It was 1960 when the 24-year-old mathematician, Margaret Hamilton took a job as a programmer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston. The reason behind her decision was not her passion for computer science. She wanted to support her husband during his three-year stint at Harvard to get a law degree. To earn money while he was at the university. Afterwards the two wanted to swap roles. She was to do her diploma in mathematics. But it never came to that. Soon Hamilton was so enthusiastic about programming and so talented in it that she was handling a plethora of projects. In her early 30s, she finally led her own team at NASA. One that pursued a mission that could hardly be bigger. It was to program the software that will land Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon. The code that made this possible is public today . It is a joint work of at least 19 men and 5 women, studded with comments. They are marked with a # at the beginning of the line – as is still commonplace in many programming languages. Then as now, these comments should explain the software's function. But they tell us more than that. They narrate the journey, personality and humour of the team. Also the questions the coders, including Margaret Hamilton ask themselves during the course of the project. «Honi soit qui mal y pense.» These are the words that precede the ignition routine of the Apollo 11 mission. And they reflect the struggle for recognition that Hamilton's team was experiencing at the beginning of the project. While the role of engineers was clear, there is not even a budget for the software department initially. Hamilton soon invents the word «software engineer», perhaps to earn more respect. And yet, a lot of it remains different with these new inventors. While classic engineers have clear processes, Hamilton and her colleagues did not. Makeshift was part of the routine of Hamilton's team. The following comment in the code also testifies to this. The author of these program lines hoped that this contribution will only be a temporary software component. However, it was actually preserved until the end. Constant improvisation was part of the everyday life of the team and also part of Hamilton's personal life. Because she not only led the software team. She was a mother, too. As both her husband and she were pursuing ambitious career plans, she brought her 4-year-old daughter Lauren along to work. While the daughter played on the office floor, the mother sat at the table coding. Time and again little Lauren started fingering the Apollo 11 control module. This was one of the reasons for the following line in the Apollo code. One day when Lauren randomly pressed some buttons, the whole simulation program suddenly crashed. Margaret Hamilton was shocked and started to search for the fault. It turned out fast: The reason for the crash was Lauren selecting the program module «P01» during the flight phase. This was part of the program that should only be executed before starting it. Realising this, Hamilton went to her superiors, and warned them of the mistake. But they turned her away saying that it was not a problem. The astronauts were excellently trained. Such an error could not happen under any circumstances. A few months later, they are taught better. During a preliminary mission of Apollo 11, Apollo 8, one of the astronauts accidentally activated «P01» in the flight phase, leading to software crash – just like the little Lauren. For hours, Hamilton and her colleagues had to feverishly search for a solution to get the program up and running again. They achieved that by adding «01521» alarm. This laid the path for always taking into account human errors in programming in the future. A school of thought that still applies today to many areas of computer science. «We realised then that nobody was perfect – not even astronauts. And so we were always looking for new ways to prepare ourselves in our response to the unexpected», Hamilton explained almost 50 years later during a lecture in 2018. In all this chaos, Hamilton and her colleagues also develop their own logic in the programming language. The idea is that the astronauts use «nouns» and «verbs» to communicate with the machine that hurls them towards the moon at a speed of over 38,000 km/h. «V16N65E», for example, stands for verb 16, noun 65 and means: Noun 65: «Time according to Apollo Guidance Computer» But if there was something else instead of «Nomen 65», the astronauts could display other things. The Shakespeare quote found in the commentary of the code seems to be based on this software principle. At the same time, a trace of fear and fatalism resonates in the words. In the «Henry 6» drama, the quote is a threat by the English rebel Cade to Lord Say. Lord Say is educated, speaks French, and is therefore falsely accused of making pacts with the French. Say's life ends when the English rebels head him, using his head as a trophy and a warning sign for enemies. Hamilton and her colleagues may also have feared certain parallels to this tragic event. She was always afraid that Hamilton would have to be the scapegoat if something went wrong: «I have always imagined the headlines in the newspapers. How they would investigate, how it came to be (disaster, note to the quote), and in the end, everyone would point their fingers at me.» But there was still time for humour in spite of all this pressure. There were jokes and curses in the software comments at one point or the other. One of them is, where the programmer hoped that this code will help the astronaut tear around the «stupid thing», namely the landing module. Lines like these indicate a casual atmosphere in the team. And so it happens that Margaret Hamilton also celebrated with her colleagues until late in the evening only to hurry back to the office thereafter as she remembered that a mistake had crept into the code. The woman who sent men to the moon with a massive pile of software would never have become a programmer by a hair's breadth . But for her husband's tiresome career plans.

What happened. It was 1960 when the 24-year-old mathematician, Margaret Hamilton took a job as a programmer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston. The reason behind her decision was not her passion for computer science. She wanted to support her husband during his three-year stint at Harvard to get a law degree. To earn money while he was at the university. Afterwards the two wanted to swap roles. She was to do her diploma in mathematics. But it never came to that.

Soon Hamilton was so enthusiastic about programming and so talented in it that she was handling a plethora of projects. In her early 30s, she finally led her own team at NASA. One that pursued a mission that could hardly be bigger. It was to program the software that will land Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon.

The code that made this possible is public today . It is a joint work of at least 19 men and 5 women, studded with comments. They are marked with a # at the beginning of the line – as is still commonplace in many programming languages. Then as now, these comments should explain the software's function. But they tell us more than that. They narrate the journey, personality and humour of the team. Also the questions the coders, including Margaret Hamilton ask themselves during the course of the project.

«Honi soit qui mal y pense.» These are the words that precede the ignition routine of the Apollo 11 mission. And they reflect the struggle for recognition that Hamilton's team was experiencing at the beginning of the project. While the role of engineers was clear, there is not even a budget for the software department initially.

Hamilton soon invents the word «software engineer», perhaps to earn more respect. And yet, a lot of it remains different with these new inventors. While classic engineers have clear processes, Hamilton and her colleagues did not. Makeshift was part of the routine of Hamilton's team. The following comment in the code also testifies to this.

The author of these program lines hoped that this contribution will only be a temporary software component. However, it was actually preserved until the end. Constant improvisation was part of the everyday life of the team and also part of Hamilton's personal life. Because she not only led the software team. She was a mother, too.

As both her husband and she were pursuing ambitious career plans, she brought her 4-year-old daughter Lauren along to work. While the daughter played on the office floor, the mother sat at the table coding. Time and again little Lauren started fingering the Apollo 11 control module. This was one of the reasons for the following line in the Apollo code.

One day when Lauren randomly pressed some buttons, the whole simulation program suddenly crashed. Margaret Hamilton was shocked and started to search for the fault. It turned out fast: The reason for the crash was Lauren selecting the program module «P01» during the flight phase. This was part of the program that should only be executed before starting it.

Realising this, Hamilton went to her superiors, and warned them of the mistake. But they turned her away saying that it was not a problem. The astronauts were excellently trained. Such an error could not happen under any circumstances. A few months later, they are taught better.

During a preliminary mission of Apollo 11, Apollo 8, one of the astronauts accidentally activated «P01» in the flight phase, leading to software crash – just like the little Lauren. For hours, Hamilton and her colleagues had to feverishly search for a solution to get the program up and running again. They achieved that by adding «01521» alarm. This laid the path for always taking into account human errors in programming in the future. A school of thought that still applies today to many areas of computer science.

«We realised then that nobody was perfect – not even astronauts. And so we were always looking for new ways to prepare ourselves in our response to the unexpected», Hamilton explained almost 50 years later during a lecture in 2018.

In all this chaos, Hamilton and her colleagues also develop their own logic in the programming language. The idea is that the astronauts use «nouns» and «verbs» to communicate with the machine that hurls them towards the moon at a speed of over 38,000 km/h. «V16N65E», for example, stands for verb 16, noun 65 and means:
Noun 65: «Time according to Apollo Guidance Computer»

But if there was something else instead of «Nomen 65», the astronauts could display other things. The Shakespeare quote found in the commentary of the code seems to be based on this software principle. At the same time, a trace of fear and fatalism resonates in the words. In the «Henry 6» drama, the quote is a threat by the English rebel Cade to Lord Say. Lord Say is educated, speaks French, and is therefore falsely accused of making pacts with the French. Say's life ends when the English rebels head him, using his head as a trophy and a warning sign for enemies.

Hamilton and her colleagues may also have feared certain parallels to this tragic event. She was always afraid that Hamilton would have to be the scapegoat if something went wrong: «I have always imagined the headlines in the newspapers. How they would investigate, how it came to be (disaster, note to the quote), and in the end, everyone would point their fingers at me.»

But there was still time for humour in spite of all this pressure. There were jokes and curses in the software comments at one point or the other. One of them is, where the programmer hoped that this code will help the astronaut tear around the «stupid thing», namely the landing module.

Lines like these indicate a casual atmosphere in the team. And so it happens that Margaret Hamilton also celebrated with her colleagues until late in the evening only to hurry back to the office thereafter as she remembered that a mistake had crept into the code.

The time had come on 28 March 1969 – three and a half months before the launch of Apollo 11. Software was ready over three years from project start. Six men approved the work of Margaret Hamilton and her team. Now the code must prove itself. High up in space.
Everything was going well for around 700’000 kilometres, and the journey to the moon was according to plan. But the calm ends when the landing approaches.
# 01201 * EXECUTIVE OVERFLOW-NO VAC AREAS EXEC BAILOUT
# 01202 * EXECUTIVE OVERFLOW-NO CORE SETS EXEC BAILOUT

The Apollo 11 system starts spitting out the error messages «1201» and «1202», which indicate system overload of the on-board computer. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin must now decide within minutes whether they should still dare the landing manoeuvre or abort the attempt and fly back to Earth without having achieved anything. What saves the mission in the end is the fact that Margaret Hamilton has also provided for such situations.

There are several solutions in the event of Apollo computer system overload. The astronauts can, for example, manually cancel certain tasks, thus reducing the computer's workload. Alternately, the computer software decides for itself which tasks have higher priority and gives them priority. A revolutionary concept for those times. And exactly the latter happens now in the landing phase.

Instead of carrying out the less important calculations for the wrongly activated rendezvous radar of the landing module «Eagle», the system software unswervingly coordinates the preparations for the landing approach. The control centre in Houston dares the risk. The astronauts are told to ignore the error messages and continue with the descent. The two astronauts finally land on the moon with fuel remaining for 30 seconds of flight time. «The Eagle Has Landed», creaks over the radio lines. And even this – thanks to Margaret Hamilton’s software.

coreStoryFacts.text: It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969
That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969.
As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen.
The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing.
Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening.
Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility.
The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing.
A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software.
Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends.
The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash.
Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission.
Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously.
Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.”
The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015.

In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight.

extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term “software engineering” and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the “Women of NASA” set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.” Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics. She ended up working for Edward Lorenz, the MIT mathematician who set out to construct a mathematical model of the weather using a set of differential equations representing changes in temperature, pressure, wind velocity, and the like. You’ve probably heard the famous story of how Lorenz kept a continuous simulation running on his LGP-30 computer, and of that fateful 1961 day when he realized that even small differences in starting values could lead to very different outcomes—a sensitivity to initial conditions that is a hallmark of chaos theory, along with strange attractors. You might not have known that it was Hamilton who was responsible for programming the LGP-30. Computers were still a novelty at the time, and neither Lorenz nor Hamilton had any programming knowledge; they taught themselves. Per a 2019 Quanta article , Lorenz was amused by her unusual methods: For instance, she once bypassed the “clunky debugging process” by rolling the paper tape down the hallway and editing the binary code by hand with a pencil. “I’d poke holes for ones, and I’d cover up with Scotch tape the others,” she recalled. Hamilton moved to another project in 1961, but not before training her replacement: a recent math graduate from Mount Holyoke named Ellen Fetter. Lorenz acknowledged the contributions of both women in his papers. In 1961, Hamilton moved to the SAGE project at MIT, writing software for a prototype XD-1 computer to aid the US Air Force in searching for possible enemy aircraft. Her first challenge: deciphering a program nobody had managed to get to work, perhaps because the author’s notes were written in Latin and Greek. Hamilton succeeded, noting with amusement that the program even printed out its answers in Greek and Latin. It was during this period that she became interested in the issue of software reliability. By 1965, Hamilton was all set to go to graduate school as planned when her husband spotted a newspaper ad saying that MIT’s Instrumentation Lab needed people to develop onboard guidance computer software for NASA’s Apollo program. She was the first programmer hired, and the first woman, working on six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972. At the time, binary code was stored using copper wires wound around cores. A “1” was a wire passing through a core, and a “0” was a wire bypassing the core. New England textile workers were hired to weave them together into long ropes, earning Hamilton the moniker “rope mother,” since she was responsible for those ropes. Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends. The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash. Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission. Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously. Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish. Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.” By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Hamilton had the idea to incorporate a failsafe into the system software’s “priority display” interface routines, should the onboard guidance computer become overloaded with more tasks than it could handle in real time. That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969. As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen. The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing. Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening. Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility. As Hamilton herself later recalled in a 1971 letter : The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing. It then sent out an alarm, which meant to the astronaut, “I’m overloaded with more tasks than I should be doing at this time and I’m going to keep only the more important tasks”; i.e., the ones needed for landing … Actually, the computer was programmed to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software. The software’s action, in this case, was to eliminate lower priority tasks and re-establish the more important ones … If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful Moon landing it was. The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015. In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight. After the Apollo program ended, the Instrumentation Lab became the independent Draper Laboratory. Hamilton worked there until 1976, when she founded Higher Order Software, based on her work on error prevention and fault tolerance. In 1985, she left the company to found Hamilton Technologies. Its main product is the Universal Systems Language (USL) for developing complex software systems that prioritized error prevention and defensive programming. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great-grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.”

Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics.

She ended up working for Edward Lorenz, the MIT mathematician who set out to construct a mathematical model of the weather using a set of differential equations representing changes in temperature, pressure, wind velocity, and the like. You’ve probably heard the famous story of how Lorenz kept a continuous simulation running on his LGP-30 computer, and of that fateful 1961 day when he realized that even small differences in starting values could lead to very different outcomes—a sensitivity to initial conditions that is a hallmark of chaos theory, along with strange attractors. You might not have known that it was Hamilton who was responsible for programming the LGP-30.

Computers were still a novelty at the time, and neither Lorenz nor Hamilton had any programming knowledge; they taught themselves. Per a 2019 Quanta article , Lorenz was amused by her unusual methods: For instance, she once bypassed the “clunky debugging process” by rolling the paper tape down the hallway and editing the binary code by hand with a pencil. “I’d poke holes for ones, and I’d cover up with Scotch tape the others,” she recalled. Hamilton moved to another project in 1961, but not before training her replacement: a recent math graduate from Mount Holyoke named Ellen Fetter. Lorenz acknowledged the contributions of both women in his papers.

In 1961, Hamilton moved to the SAGE project at MIT, writing software for a prototype XD-1 computer to aid the US Air Force in searching for possible enemy aircraft. Her first challenge: deciphering a program nobody had managed to get to work, perhaps because the author’s notes were written in Latin and Greek. Hamilton succeeded, noting with amusement that the program even printed out its answers in Greek and Latin. It was during this period that she became interested in the issue of software reliability.

By 1965, Hamilton was all set to go to graduate school as planned when her husband spotted a newspaper ad saying that MIT’s Instrumentation Lab needed people to develop onboard guidance computer software for NASA’s Apollo program. She was the first programmer hired, and the first woman, working on six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972. At the time, binary code was stored using copper wires wound around cores. A “1” was a wire passing through a core, and a “0” was a wire bypassing the core. New England textile workers were hired to weave them together into long ropes, earning Hamilton the moniker “rope mother,” since she was responsible for those ropes.

Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends. The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash. Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission. Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously. Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish. Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.”

By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Hamilton had the idea to incorporate a failsafe into the system software’s “priority display” interface routines, should the onboard guidance computer become overloaded with more tasks than it could handle in real time.

That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969. As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen. The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing. Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening. Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility.
As Hamilton herself later recalled in a 1971 letter :

The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing. It then sent out an alarm, which meant to the astronaut, “I’m overloaded with more tasks than I should be doing at this time and I’m going to keep only the more important tasks”; i.e., the ones needed for landing … Actually, the computer was programmed to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software. The software’s action, in this case, was to eliminate lower priority tasks and re-establish the more important ones … If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful Moon landing it was.

The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015. In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight.

After the Apollo program ended, the Instrumentation Lab became the independent Draper Laboratory. Hamilton worked there until 1976, when she founded Higher Order Software, based on her work on error prevention and fault tolerance. In 1985, she left the company to found Hamilton Technologies. Its main product is the Universal Systems Language (USL) for developing complex software systems that prioritized error prevention and defensive programming.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great-grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn.

The woman who sent men to the moon with a massive pile of software would never have become a programmer by a hair's breadth . But for her husband's tiresome career plans. What happened. It was 1960 when the 24-year-old mathematician, Margaret Hamilton took a job as a programmer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston. The reason behind her decision was not her passion for computer science. She wanted to support her husband during his three-year stint at Harvard to get a law degree. To earn money while he was at the university. Afterwards the two wanted to swap roles. She was to do her diploma in mathematics. But it never came to that. Soon Hamilton was so enthusiastic about programming and so talented in it that she was handling a plethora of projects. In her early 30s, she finally led her own team at NASA. One that pursued a mission that could hardly be bigger. It was to program the software that will land Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon. The code that made this possible is public today . It is a joint work of at least 19 men and 5 women, studded with comments. They are marked with a # at the beginning of the line – as is still commonplace in many programming languages. Then as now, these comments should explain the software's function. But they tell us more than that. They narrate the journey, personality and humour of the team. Also the questions the coders, including Margaret Hamilton ask themselves during the course of the project. «Honi soit qui mal y pense.» These are the words that precede the ignition routine of the Apollo 11 mission. And they reflect the struggle for recognition that Hamilton's team was experiencing at the beginning of the project. While the role of engineers was clear, there is not even a budget for the software department initially. Hamilton soon invents the word «software engineer», perhaps to earn more respect. And yet, a lot of it remains different with these new inventors. While classic engineers have clear processes, Hamilton and her colleagues did not. Makeshift was part of the routine of Hamilton's team. The following comment in the code also testifies to this. The author of these program lines hoped that this contribution will only be a temporary software component. However, it was actually preserved until the end. Constant improvisation was part of the everyday life of the team and also part of Hamilton's personal life. Because she not only led the software team. She was a mother, too. As both her husband and she were pursuing ambitious career plans, she brought her 4-year-old daughter Lauren along to work. While the daughter played on the office floor, the mother sat at the table coding. Time and again little Lauren started fingering the Apollo 11 control module. This was one of the reasons for the following line in the Apollo code. One day when Lauren randomly pressed some buttons, the whole simulation program suddenly crashed. Margaret Hamilton was shocked and started to search for the fault. It turned out fast: The reason for the crash was Lauren selecting the program module «P01» during the flight phase. This was part of the program that should only be executed before starting it. Realising this, Hamilton went to her superiors, and warned them of the mistake. But they turned her away saying that it was not a problem. The astronauts were excellently trained. Such an error could not happen under any circumstances. A few months later, they are taught better. During a preliminary mission of Apollo 11, Apollo 8, one of the astronauts accidentally activated «P01» in the flight phase, leading to software crash – just like the little Lauren. For hours, Hamilton and her colleagues had to feverishly search for a solution to get the program up and running again. They achieved that by adding «01521» alarm. This laid the path for always taking into account human errors in programming in the future. A school of thought that still applies today to many areas of computer science. «We realised then that nobody was perfect – not even astronauts. And so we were always looking for new ways to prepare ourselves in our response to the unexpected», Hamilton explained almost 50 years later during a lecture in 2018. In all this chaos, Hamilton and her colleagues also develop their own logic in the programming language. The idea is that the astronauts use «nouns» and «verbs» to communicate with the machine that hurls them towards the moon at a speed of over 38,000 km/h. «V16N65E», for example, stands for verb 16, noun 65 and means: Noun 65: «Time according to Apollo Guidance Computer» But if there was something else instead of «Nomen 65», the astronauts could display other things. The Shakespeare quote found in the commentary of the code seems to be based on this software principle. At the same time, a trace of fear and fatalism resonates in the words. In the «Henry 6» drama, the quote is a threat by the English rebel Cade to Lord Say. Lord Say is educated, speaks French, and is therefore falsely accused of making pacts with the French. Say's life ends when the English rebels head him, using his head as a trophy and a warning sign for enemies. Hamilton and her colleagues may also have feared certain parallels to this tragic event. She was always afraid that Hamilton would have to be the scapegoat if something went wrong: «I have always imagined the headlines in the newspapers. How they would investigate, how it came to be (disaster, note to the quote), and in the end, everyone would point their fingers at me.» But there was still time for humour in spite of all this pressure. There were jokes and curses in the software comments at one point or the other. One of them is, where the programmer hoped that this code will help the astronaut tear around the «stupid thing», namely the landing module. Lines like these indicate a casual atmosphere in the team. And so it happens that Margaret Hamilton also celebrated with her colleagues until late in the evening only to hurry back to the office thereafter as she remembered that a mistake had crept into the code. RAGAN The time had come on 28 March 1969 – three and a half months before the launch of Apollo 11. Software was ready over three years from project start. Six men approved the work of Margaret Hamilton and her team. Now the code must prove itself. High up in space. The woman who sent men to the moon with a massive pile of software would never have become a programmer by a hair's breadth . But for her husband's tiresome career plans.

What happened. It was 1960 when the 24-year-old mathematician, Margaret Hamilton took a job as a programmer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston. The reason behind her decision was not her passion for computer science. She wanted to support her husband during his three-year stint at Harvard to get a law degree. To earn money while he was at the university. Afterwards the two wanted to swap roles. She was to do her diploma in mathematics. But it never came to that.

Soon Hamilton was so enthusiastic about programming and so talented in it that she was handling a plethora of projects. In her early 30s, she finally led her own team at NASA. One that pursued a mission that could hardly be bigger. It was to program the software that will land Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon.

The code that made this possible is public today . It is a joint work of at least 19 men and 5 women, studded with comments. They are marked with a # at the beginning of the line – as is still commonplace in many programming languages. Then as now, these comments should explain the software's function. But they tell us more than that. They narrate the journey, personality and humour of the team. Also the questions the coders, including Margaret Hamilton ask themselves during the course of the project.

«Honi soit qui mal y pense.» These are the words that precede the ignition routine of the Apollo 11 mission. And they reflect the struggle for recognition that Hamilton's team was experiencing at the beginning of the project. While the role of engineers was clear, there is not even a budget for the software department initially.

Hamilton soon invents the word «software engineer», perhaps to earn more respect. And yet, a lot of it remains different with these new inventors. While classic engineers have clear processes, Hamilton and her colleagues did not. Makeshift was part of the routine of Hamilton's team. The following comment in the code also testifies to this.

The author of these program lines hoped that this contribution will only be a temporary software component. However, it was actually preserved until the end. Constant improvisation was part of the everyday life of the team and also part of Hamilton's personal life. Because she not only led the software team. She was a mother, too.

As both her husband and she were pursuing ambitious career plans, she brought her 4-year-old daughter Lauren along to work. While the daughter played on the office floor, the mother sat at the table coding. Time and again little Lauren started fingering the Apollo 11 control module. This was one of the reasons for the following line in the Apollo code.

One day when Lauren randomly pressed some buttons, the whole simulation program suddenly crashed. Margaret Hamilton was shocked and started to search for the fault. It turned out fast: The reason for the crash was Lauren selecting the program module «P01» during the flight phase. This was part of the program that should only be executed before starting it.

Realising this, Hamilton went to her superiors, and warned them of the mistake. But they turned her away saying that it was not a problem. The astronauts were excellently trained. Such an error could not happen under any circumstances. A few months later, they are taught better.

During a preliminary mission of Apollo 11, Apollo 8, one of the astronauts accidentally activated «P01» in the flight phase, leading to software crash – just like the little Lauren. For hours, Hamilton and her colleagues had to feverishly search for a solution to get the program up and running again. They achieved that by adding «01521» alarm. This laid the path for always taking into account human errors in programming in the future. A school of thought that still applies today to many areas of computer science.

«We realised then that nobody was perfect – not even astronauts. And so we were always looking for new ways to prepare ourselves in our response to the unexpected», Hamilton explained almost 50 years later during a lecture in 2018.

In all this chaos, Hamilton and her colleagues also develop their own logic in the programming language. The idea is that the astronauts use «nouns» and «verbs» to communicate with the machine that hurls them towards the moon at a speed of over 38,000 km/h. «V16N65E», for example, stands for verb 16, noun 65 and means:
Noun 65: «Time according to Apollo Guidance Computer»

But if there was something else instead of «Nomen 65», the astronauts could display other things. The Shakespeare quote found in the commentary of the code seems to be based on this software principle. At the same time, a trace of fear and fatalism resonates in the words. In the «Henry 6» drama, the quote is a threat by the English rebel Cade to Lord Say. Lord Say is educated, speaks French, and is therefore falsely accused of making pacts with the French. Say's life ends when the English rebels head him, using his head as a trophy and a warning sign for enemies.

Hamilton and her colleagues may also have feared certain parallels to this tragic event. She was always afraid that Hamilton would have to be the scapegoat if something went wrong: «I have always imagined the headlines in the newspapers. How they would investigate, how it came to be (disaster, note to the quote), and in the end, everyone would point their fingers at me.»

But there was still time for humour in spite of all this pressure. There were jokes and curses in the software comments at one point or the other. One of them is, where the programmer hoped that this code will help the astronaut tear around the «stupid thing», namely the landing module.

Lines like these indicate a casual atmosphere in the team. And so it happens that Margaret Hamilton also celebrated with her colleagues until late in the evening only to hurry back to the office thereafter as she remembered that a mistake had crept into the code.

The time had come on 28 March 1969 – three and a half months before the launch of Apollo 11. Software was ready over three years from project start. Six men approved the work of Margaret Hamilton and her team. Now the code must prove itself. High up in space.
Everything was going well for around 700’000 kilometres, and the journey to the moon was according to plan. But the calm ends when the landing approaches.
# 01201 * EXECUTIVE OVERFLOW-NO VAC AREAS EXEC BAILOUT
# 01202 * EXECUTIVE OVERFLOW-NO CORE SETS EXEC BAILOUT

What saves the mission in the end is the fact that Margaret Hamilton has also provided for such situations.

There are several solutions in the event of Apollo computer system overload. The astronauts can, for example, manually cancel certain tasks, thus reducing the computer's workload. Alternately, the computer software decides for itself which tasks have higher priority and gives them priority. A revolutionary concept for those times. And exactly the latter happens now in the landing phase.

Instead of carrying out the less important calculations for the wrongly activated rendezvous radar of the landing module «Eagle», the system software unswervingly coordinates the preparations for the landing approach. The control centre in Houston dares the risk. The astronauts are told to ignore the error messages and continue with the descent. The two astronauts finally land on the moon with fuel remaining for 30 seconds of flight time. «The Eagle Has Landed», creaks over the radio lines. And even this – thanks to Margaret Hamilton’s software.

facts.text: It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969
That’s exactly what happened on the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969.
As the Eagle lunar module approached the Moon, Buzz Aldrin entered the codes to display altitude and other relevant data on the screen.
The onboard computer started flashing alarms, forcing Mission Control to consider aborting the landing.
Hamilton’s fail-safe meant that the computer was prioritizing essential tasks and canceling nonessential ones, and the alarm was to let astronauts know that this was happening.
Thanks to Hamilton’s foresight, Eagle still safely landed on the Sea of Tranquility.
The computer (or rather the software in it) was smart enough to recognize that it was being asked to perform more tasks than it should be performing.
A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software.
Hamilton would often bring her 4-year-old daughter, Lauren, to the lab on nights and weekends.
The child loved pretending to be an astronaut in the simulators, and one day her random button-pressing caused the system to inexplicably crash.
Apparently Lauren had typed “P01,” a pre-launch sequence, in the middle of the mission.
Hamilton asked NASA if she could add a safeguard to prevent this from happening on an actual mission, but the higher-ups didn’t take it seriously.
Then astronaut Jim Lovell actually made that error during the Apollo 8 manned mission to orbit the Moon, causing the navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton was called in to retrieve the data, jokingly referring to this as the “Lauren bug.”
The Apollo software she helped develop was added to GitHub in 2015.

In 2019, Google marked the 50th anniversary of the Moon landing—and Hamilton’s crucial contribution—by training over 100,000 mirrors at its Mojave Desert solar power farm to create a massive portrait of Hamilton in reflected moonlight.

passages: Editor’s note: Below is an edited transcript of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks at Google I/O 2026, adapted to include more of what was announced on stage.
See all the announcements in our collection .
Another place where we’ve been rapidly innovating is in the Gemini app .
Today, we’ve surpassed 900 million, more than doubling in a year.
In that same time, daily requests have grown over seven times.
Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities.
With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals.
These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge.
Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models.
We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities.
You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today.
Gemini Omni Flash is available starting today.
We'll also be rolling it out to developers and enterprise customers via APIs in the coming weeks.
Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.
Gemini Omni is our new model that is capable of generating samples in any output modality from any input.
We’re starting with video outputs, and over time we’ll enable image and text.
This new model combines Gemini’s intelligence with our generative media models — a huge leap forward in world understanding.
I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction.
Here’s how we’re helping you get more done with Gemini.
There’s also a lot of latent productivity to be unlocked.
Recently, Maps got its biggest upgrade in a decade, including a new feature called Ask Maps .
People are using Ask Maps for more complex, and much longer questions.
And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products.
This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools.
It all starts with Search , which is bringing the benefits of generative AI to more people than any other product in the world.

extraction.body: At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.
