coreStoryFacts.text: Editor’s note: Below is an edited transcript of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks at Google I/O 2026, adapted to include more of what was announced on stage.
See all the announcements in our collection .
Another place where we’ve been rapidly innovating is in the Gemini app .
Today, we’ve surpassed 900 million, more than doubling in a year.
In that same time, daily requests have grown over seven times.
Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities.
With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals.
These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge.
Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models.
We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities.
You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today.
Gemini Omni Flash is available starting today.
We'll also be rolling it out to developers and enterprise customers via APIs in the coming weeks.
Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.
Gemini Omni is our new model that is capable of generating samples in any output modality from any input.
We’re starting with video outputs, and over time we’ll enable image and text.
This new model combines Gemini’s intelligence with our generative media models — a huge leap forward in world understanding.
I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction.
Here’s how we’re helping you get more done with Gemini.
There’s also a lot of latent productivity to be unlocked.
Recently, Maps got its biggest upgrade in a decade, including a new feature called Ask Maps .
People are using Ask Maps for more complex, and much longer questions.
And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products.
This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools.

extraction.body: At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. Trump said he wants 40% to 50% of global chip production on American soil by the end of his term.
Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has warned that people who continue to use the term "Artificial Intelligence" instead of his preferred phrase "Super Intelligence" will be considered enemies, escalating his campaign to replace the widely used terminology for the technology. According to The Independent, Trump made the declaration in a Truth Social post on Thursday, saying the White House "considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" The remarks follow an executive order he signed just over a week ago directing executive branch agencies to use "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" in government communications. The order came after Trump met technology industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai and Dario Amodei, at a White House lunch. Trump had also promoted the terminology during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, where he rejected international efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and said the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake." "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," Trump said. A week earlier, he had launched a poll on Truth Social asking users to choose between "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," and "Extreme Intelligence." Trump's push to popularise the new term comes as public opinion polls indicate widespread concern about artificial intelligence and its growing infrastructure in the United States. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters conducted late last month found that 73% opposed building an AI data centre in their community, including 55% of Republicans. The survey also found that 79% believed safety should take priority over keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Only 25% approved of Trump's handling of the technology, while 58% disapproved. Meanwhile, 71% said they would be more likely to support a political candidate who backed "stricter guardrails" on AI. That included 52% of Republicans and nearly three-quarters of independent voters. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September found that 37% viewed AI favourably, compared with 60% who viewed it unfavourably. The technology's net favourability rating had deteriorated to minus 23, from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle AI data centres by 14 percentage points. Among voters opposed to such facilities in any location, Democrats led the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump's latest demand follows other efforts to impose his preferred terminology on government communications and geographical names. Just over a month ago, he issued an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America". The move came amid tensions with Canada over trade and followed his earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". While the president can direct how the US government refers to geographical features and landmarks, he cannot compel Canada or individual citizens to adopt his preferred names. The same limitation applies to "super intelligence": Trump can instruct federal agencies to use the phrase, but he cannot force Americans or people elsewhere to abandon the established term "artificial intelligence". The Independent contacted NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic to ask whether they planned to adopt the terminology in promotional materials or customer communications. None responded, according to the report. The White House, however, has highlighted several technology executives who have used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang. The proposed terminology also carries a distinct technical meaning. Superintelligence generally refers to an AI system capable of surpassing human intellectual abilities across multiple fields, including reasoning, social skills and scientific research. The concept is often discussed in debates over advanced AI systems, including concerns about their potential risks and the need for safeguards and emergency shutdown mechanisms. Replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government communications does not, by itself, change the technology's capabilities or its established technical meaning. The remarks follow an executive order he signed just over a week ago directing executive branch agencies to use "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" in government communications.
The order came after Trump met technology industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai and Dario Amodei, at a White House lunch.

Trump had also promoted the terminology during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, where he rejected international efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and said the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake."
"It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," Trump said.
A week earlier, he had launched a poll on Truth Social asking users to choose between "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," and "Extreme Intelligence."
Trump's push to popularise the new term comes as public opinion polls indicate widespread concern about artificial intelligence and its growing infrastructure in the United States.

A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters conducted late last month found that 73% opposed building an AI data centre in their community, including 55% of Republicans. The survey also found that 79% believed safety should take priority over keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development.

Only 25% approved of Trump's handling of the technology, while 58% disapproved. Meanwhile, 71% said they would be more likely to support a political candidate who backed "stricter guardrails" on AI. That included 52% of Republicans and nearly three-quarters of independent voters.

A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September found that 37% viewed AI favourably, compared with 60% who viewed it unfavourably. The technology's net favourability rating had deteriorated to minus 23, from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July.

The same survey found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle AI data centres by 14 percentage points. Among voters opposed to such facilities in any location, Democrats led the generic ballot by at least 19 points.
Trump's latest demand follows other efforts to impose his preferred terminology on government communications and geographical names.

Just over a month ago, he issued an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America". The move came amid tensions with Canada over trade and followed his earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America".
While the president can direct how the US government refers to geographical features and landmarks, he cannot compel Canada or individual citizens to adopt his preferred names.

The same limitation applies to "super intelligence": Trump can instruct federal agencies to use the phrase, but he cannot force Americans or people elsewhere to abandon the established term "artificial intelligence".

The Independent contacted NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic to ask whether they planned to adopt the terminology in promotional materials or customer communications. None responded, according to the report.
The White House, however, has highlighted several technology executives who have used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang.

The proposed terminology also carries a distinct technical meaning. Superintelligence generally refers to an AI system capable of surpassing human intellectual abilities across multiple fields, including reasoning, social skills and scientific research.
The concept is often discussed in debates over advanced AI systems, including concerns about their potential risks and the need for safeguards and emergency shutdown mechanisms.
Replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government communications does not, by itself, change the technology's capabilities or its established technical meaning.

Trump said he wants 40% to 50% of global chip production on American soil by the end of his term.
Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance.
On the arms package: "I haven't approved it yet.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump delivered notably different messages about Taiwan within the same 24-hour period.

Rubio told NBC News late Thursday that U.S. policy is "unchanged as of today," warned it would be "a terrible mistake" for China to use force, and said there would be global "repercussions" if Beijing moved militarily.

Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan.

Taiwan's foreign ministry declared the island a "sovereign and independent democratic nation" on Saturday, stating that it is "not subordinate to the People's Republic of China.” The statement came hours after President Donald Trump, wrapping up a two-day state visit to Beijing, told Fox News he opposes Taiwan pursuing formal independence, described a pending $14 billion arms package as a "very good negotiating chip," and repeated his claim that Taiwan "stole" the U.S. semiconductor industry. Trump said he wants 40% to 50% of global chip production on American soil by the end of his term. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump delivered notably different messages about Taiwan within the same 24-hour period. Rubio told NBC News late Thursday that U.S. policy is "unchanged as of today," warned it would be "a terrible mistake" for China to use force, and said there would be global "repercussions" if Beijing moved militarily. Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance. He questioned why the U.S. would travel 9,500 miles to fight a war and called Taiwan "a very small island" 59 miles from mainland China. On the arms package: "I haven't approved it yet. We're going to see what happens," he said. Chinese President Xi Jinping had opened the summit by warning that mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to "clashes and even conflicts.” Trump, meanwhile, has previously called Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance a form of theft, and on Friday, he reiterated that he wanted all of the island's chipmakers to move to the United States. That demand sits alongside an already-signed trade deal in which Taiwan committed $500 billion in U.S. semiconductor investment for reduced tariffs, with TSMC alone pledging $165 billion toward Arizona fab expansion. Taiwan's parliament also approved a $25 billion defense budget, with roughly $9 billion covering the first tranche of the December arms package and a second phase worth over $15 billion still awaiting U.S. approval. Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan. Uncertainty over U.S. security commitments could reinforce that stance because Taiwan's semiconductor leverage is most valuable when production remains concentrated on the island. Taiwan's Presidential Office highlighted "multiple reaffirmations" from both Trump and Rubio that U.S. policy remains unchanged, with spokeswoman Karen Kuo saying Taipei looks forward to continued cooperation "under the firm commitments of the Taiwan Relations Act.” The foreign ministry separately called arms sales a form of "joint deterrence against regional threats." Trump said he wants 40% to 50% of global chip production on American soil by the end of his term.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump delivered notably different messages about Taiwan within the same 24-hour period. Rubio told NBC News late Thursday that U.S. policy is "unchanged as of today," warned it would be "a terrible mistake" for China to use force, and said there would be global "repercussions" if Beijing moved militarily.

Trump, in a Fox News interview taped Friday in Beijing, took a markedly different stance. He questioned why the U.S. would travel 9,500 miles to fight a war and called Taiwan "a very small island" 59 miles from mainland China. On the arms package: "I haven't approved it yet. We're going to see what happens," he said.

Chinese President Xi Jinping had opened the summit by warning that mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to "clashes and even conflicts.” Trump, meanwhile, has previously called Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance a form of theft, and on Friday, he reiterated that he wanted all of the island's chipmakers to move to the United States.

That demand sits alongside an already-signed trade deal in which Taiwan committed $500 billion in U.S. semiconductor investment for reduced tariffs, with TSMC alone pledging $165 billion toward Arizona fab expansion. Taiwan's parliament also approved a $25 billion defense budget, with roughly $9 billion covering the first tranche of the December arms package and a second phase worth over $15 billion still awaiting U.S. approval.

Taiwan has already rejected Washington's push to transfer half of its advanced chipmaking capacity to U.S. soil and restricted TSMC from producing its most advanced process nodes outside Taiwan. Uncertainty over U.S. security commitments could reinforce that stance because Taiwan's semiconductor leverage is most valuable when production remains concentrated on the island.

Taiwan's Presidential Office highlighted "multiple reaffirmations" from both Trump and Rubio that U.S. policy remains unchanged, with spokeswoman Karen Kuo saying Taipei looks forward to continued cooperation "under the firm commitments of the Taiwan Relations Act.” The foreign ministry separately called arms sales a form of "joint deterrence against regional threats."

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has warned that people who continue to use the term "Artificial Intelligence" instead of his preferred phrase "Super Intelligence" will be considered enemies, escalating his campaign to replace the widely used terminology for the technology. According to The Independent, Trump made the declaration in a Truth Social post on Thursday, saying the White House "considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" The remarks follow an executive order he signed just over a week ago directing executive branch agencies to use "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" in government communications. The order came after Trump met technology industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai and Dario Amodei, at a White House lunch. Trump had also promoted the terminology during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, where he rejected international efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and said the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake." "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," Trump said. A week earlier, he had launched a poll on Truth Social asking users to choose between "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," and "Extreme Intelligence." Trump's push to popularise the new term comes as public opinion polls indicate widespread concern about artificial intelligence and its growing infrastructure in the United States. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters conducted late last month found that 73% opposed building an AI data centre in their community, including 55% of Republicans. The survey also found that 79% believed safety should take priority over keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Only 25% approved of Trump's handling of the technology, while 58% disapproved. Meanwhile, 71% said they would be more likely to support a political candidate who backed "stricter guardrails" on AI. That included 52% of Republicans and nearly three-quarters of independent voters. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September found that 37% viewed AI favourably, compared with 60% who viewed it unfavourably. The technology's net favourability rating had deteriorated to minus 23, from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle AI data centres by 14 percentage points. Among voters opposed to such facilities in any location, Democrats led the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump's latest demand follows other efforts to impose his preferred terminology on government communications and geographical names. Just over a month ago, he issued an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America". The move came amid tensions with Canada over trade and followed his earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". While the president can direct how the US government refers to geographical features and landmarks, he cannot compel Canada or individual citizens to adopt his preferred names. The same limitation applies to "super intelligence": Trump can instruct federal agencies to use the phrase, but he cannot force Americans or people elsewhere to abandon the established term "artificial intelligence". The Independent contacted NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic to ask whether they planned to adopt the terminology in promotional materials or customer communications. None responded, according to the report. The White House, however, has highlighted several technology executives who have used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang. The proposed terminology also carries a distinct technical meaning. Superintelligence generally refers to an AI system capable of surpassing human intellectual abilities across multiple fields, including reasoning, social skills and scientific research. The concept is often discussed in debates over advanced AI systems, including concerns about their potential risks and the need for safeguards and emergency shutdown mechanisms. Replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government communications does not, by itself, change the technology's capabilities or its established technical meaning. extraction.body: Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner. It says open-source projects that opt-in will get “thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.” That could mean open-source projects get alerted about possible security issues sooner, but the trade-off is that OSS Scanner’s reports don’t come with human review: > The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage. OSS Scanner is far from the first AI bug hunting helper out there. AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May. At the same time, some open-source projects are struggling to keep up with the sudden onslaught of AI-generated bug reports, including Linus Torvalds and even Google.

passages: OSS Scanner , launched with it, offers open-source projects free periodic vulnerability scans from the company’s strongest models.
Both fall under a new effort Anthropic calls the Anthropic Cyber Mission.
Of the more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities its models turned up in widely used software over the past six months, staff have manually reviewed about 6,000.
A growing number of maintainers who received early reports asked for the whole unreviewed batch, proposed patches included, and nearly 5,000 such reports have gone out so far.
OSS Scanner turns that arrangement into a standing service for other eligible projects.
To gauge how often that happens, Anthropic tested the scanner’s accuracy before opening it to more projects.
Core maintainers can enroll by submitting a pull request to an Anthropic GitHub repository.
Eligibility follows the OSS-Fuzz test of “critical impact on infrastructure and user security,” with decisions made case by case.
Projects without the staff to keep up with raw findings will still get human-verified reports through Anthropic’s existing disclosure process.
Anthropic PBC today launched a program that brings its frontier models and onsite engineers to the security companies protecting power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure.
The Defender Advantage Fund that Anthropic set up in August pays to keep the scanner free.
The company has also put money into the Python Software Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation.
The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program starts with the outside providers that operators of every size already rely on for advice on which fixes are safe to apply to a running system.
The program is aimed at operational technology in plants, substations and water systems, where equipment built to run for decades often cannot be taken offline for a patch.
Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and to help their customers do the same.
More partners and sectors are due to join over the coming months.
The announcement leaves out the commercial terms.
Axios noted in its coverage that Anthropic has not said whether partners get free model access or who covers the computing costs.
The same report questioned how partners will test and deploy fixes without disrupting utility operations.
Both launches draw on lessons from Project Glasswing.

extraction.body: Anthropic PBC today launched a program that brings its frontier models and onsite engineers to the security companies protecting power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure. OSS Scanner , launched with it, offers open-source projects free periodic vulnerability scans from the company’s strongest models. Both fall under a new effort Anthropic calls the Anthropic Cyber Mission. The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program starts with the outside providers that operators of every size already rely on for advice on which fixes are safe to apply to a running system. Eleven of those providers signed on as founding partners. Accenture plc, Booz Allen Hamilton Inc., Deloitte & Touche LLP and PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP come from the consulting side, where they run security programs for operators. Security vendors make up the biggest bloc, with industrial specialists Dragos Inc., Insane Cyber Inc. and Nozomi Networks Inc. joining CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. and Palo Alto Networks Inc. Hitachi Ltd. and Rockwell Automation Inc. build and patch the hardware itself. The program is aimed at operational technology in plants, substations and water systems, where equipment built to run for decades often cannot be taken offline for a patch. Known flaws can sit there for years. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and to help their customers do the same. More partners and sectors are due to join over the coming months. Andrew Turner, president of commercial cyber at Booz Allen, called operational technology “the next frontier for autonomous AI-enabled attacks” in comments published with the announcement. What matters now, he said, is how much control artificial intelligence can gain over an industrial process and how fast. The announcement leaves out the commercial terms. Axios noted in its coverage that Anthropic has not said whether partners get free model access or who covers the computing costs. The same report questioned how partners will test and deploy fixes without disrupting utility operations. The open-source half of today’s news grew out of a backlog in Anthropic’s own disclosure work. Of the more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities its models turned up in widely used software over the past six months, staff have manually reviewed about 6,000. A growing number of maintainers who received early reports asked for the whole unreviewed batch, proposed patches included, and nearly 5,000 such reports have gone out so far. OSS Scanner turns that arrangement into a standing service for other eligible projects. Google LLC’s OSS-Fuzz, which runs fuzzers against open-source code, inspired the setup. Every report includes a self-contained reproducer. Early tester Anton Arapov of the OpenSSL Corporation said a report with a real exploit attached is “basically job done for an engineer.” Where the model can manage it, a candidate patch comes with the write-up, and a bisection of the code history shows when the flaw was introduced. Reports from the new service go straight to maintainers without human review so they arrive faster. Some will contain mistakes as a result, such as a wrong severity rating, Anthropic said. To gauge how often that happens, Anthropic tested the scanner’s accuracy before opening it to more projects. The expert penetration testers who vet the company’s coordinated disclosures checked 97 critical and high-severity findings from an early version across 48 projects and cleared 85 for disclosure. Of the other 12, all but one were real bugs that duplicated known issues or other findings from the scan. Embedded encryption library developer wolfSSL Inc. said all but two of the 74 reports it received during early trials were valid and that five became CVEs. Core maintainers can enroll by submitting a pull request to an Anthropic GitHub repository. Eligibility follows the OSS-Fuzz test of “critical impact on infrastructure and user security,” with decisions made case by case. Projects without the staff to keep up with raw findings will still get human-verified reports through Anthropic’s existing disclosure process. The Defender Advantage Fund that Anthropic set up in August pays to keep the scanner free. The company has also put money into the Python Software Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation. Both launches draw on lessons from Project Glasswing. That program gave vetted organizations access to Claude Mythos from April until it was folded into an expanded Cyber Verification Program earlier this week . Finding vulnerabilities has never been easier, according to Anthropic. Verifying, prioritizing and fixing them remains hard, and the company said Glasswing has not yet cut cyber risk by enough. Anthropic expects AI to favor defenders within two years. For now the cost of exploiting a flaw keeps falling, and verifying and repairing one is still slow work that depends on people. With operational technology, a fix may have to wait until it can go safely onto running machinery, and in rare cases that could take decades. sources.title: Anthropic offers free AI security scans for open source as Claude Code faces scrutiny - Startup Fortune
passages: The news here is the next step down from Glasswing's institutional scale: free, self-serve access for ordinary open-source maintainers, not just the handful of large foundations invited into the pilot.

Maintainers can apply for expedited access to run full-repository or targeted-directory scans that trace how data moves through their code, flag weaknesses across interconnected components, and generate draft patches for review.

Each finding goes through what Anthropic describes as a multi-stage verification pipeline before it reaches a human: an attempt to cut down the false-positive noise that has plagued automated scanners for years.
A companion Claude Security plugin for Claude Code, now in beta, adds a simple slash command that launches a team of Claude agents against your changes before you commit.
On October 3, Yonhap reported that South Korea's Shinhan Bank was investigating a breach.
Early findings point to AI tools used to automate credential-stuffing attacks against a service used by loan recruiters.

Within days, researchers tied infrastructure linked to the broader wave of South Korean bank intrusions to ARTEX AI: a Chinese open-source penetration-testing framework that automates vulnerability discovery and attack-path planning.
The wave also touched KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan and several smaller lenders.

Separately, Security Affairs reported on a distinct campaign in which Claude Code and DeepSeek were used together to automate intrusions against government and financial targets, handling exploit reasoning and building phishing pages.
Anthropic's own coding agent, in other words, has become raw material for attackers whether or not it was the tool used in any single breach.
Dual-use is the nature of the technology, and Chainalysis-style arguments about banning tools because criminals use them apply just as well to language models as they once did to cryptocurrency.
Anthropic is betting that free scans and a public vulnerability count will do more to shape the narrative than any statement could.
For maintainers deciding whether to hand over their repositories, the real test isn't whether Claude can find bugs.
Project Glasswing's numbers say it clearly can.
It's whether Anthropic will say, in plain terms, what happens to the code once it does.
Anthropic's answer has been building for most of the year, and it did not start this month.
Claude Code Security launched in February as a limited research preview for Enterprise and Team customers.
It was built on Claude Opus 4.6 to trace data flow and component relationships across a codebase, rather than pattern-match the way Snyk, GitHub's CodeQL or Dependabot do.

Then, by May, Anthropic scaled the idea up dramatically with Project Glasswing: an initiative that paired an unreleased model called Claude Mythos Preview with AWS, Google, Microsoft, Cisco, CrowdStrike, JPMorganChase and the Linux Foundation to hunt bugs across critical open-source infrastructure.
Glasswing found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities in its first month alone, according to a report from Forklog.
The project's cumulative tally has since passed 23,000 findings across more than 1,000 projects, touching software as widely used as NGINX, jq, Mastodon, ImageMagick, FreeRDP and MinIO.
Anthropic says it confirmed 90.6% of what the model flagged.
The pitch: let the model that can break code also be the one that finds the holes first.
None of that answers the harder question hanging over the announcement: what does Anthropic actually see when it scans your repository?
The company has not published detailed terms on data retention or whether scan results, or the code itself, feed back into model training.
A free tool that reads your entire codebase is also a tool that, by definition, has your entire codebase.
Independent comparisons published earlier this year found Claude Security takes minutes per scan, not the seconds a rule-based tool like CodeQL needs.
Axios reports that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents involving their AI models and agents, most never disclosed publicly.

The finding follows a month of individual failures, from a DNS-based sandbox escape at OpenAI to a nine-zero-day breach of Hugging Face, and raises hard questions about whether any... - how AI models escape sandbox security measures - anthropic and openai security incident investigation details
Anthropic has named Accenture its first embedded AI safety evaluator, giving the consulting giant's Faculty unit employee-level access to red-team its models.

story.title: Anthropic launches free AI security scans for open-source projects

facts.text: Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner.
AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May.
Anthropic has announced the launch of free AI security scans specifically designed for open-source projects, as reported by The Verge.
This new offering is part of Anthropic’s broader Anthropic Cyber Mission initiative.
The service provides model-generated reports that identify potential vulnerabilities without human review or triage.
As of now, the likelihood of Anthropic having the best AI model by the end of November 2026 has seen fluctuations, with recent odds priced at 40% for a YES outcome.
© Decentral Media and Crypto Briefing® 2026.
OSS Scanner , launched with it, offers open-source projects free periodic vulnerability scans from the company’s strongest models.
Both fall under a new effort Anthropic calls the Anthropic Cyber Mission.
Of the more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities its models turned up in widely used software over the past six months, staff have manually reviewed about 6,000.
A growing number of maintainers who received early reports asked for the whole unreviewed batch, proposed patches included, and nearly 5,000 such reports have gone out so far.
OSS Scanner turns that arrangement into a standing service for other eligible projects.
To gauge how often that happens, Anthropic tested the scanner’s accuracy before opening it to more projects.
Core maintainers can enroll by submitting a pull request to an Anthropic GitHub repository.
Eligibility follows the OSS-Fuzz test of “critical impact on infrastructure and user security,” with decisions made case by case.
Projects without the staff to keep up with raw findings will still get human-verified reports through Anthropic’s existing disclosure process.
Anthropic PBC today launched a program that brings its frontier models and onsite engineers to the security companies protecting power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure.
The Defender Advantage Fund that Anthropic set up in August pays to keep the scanner free.
The company has also put money into the Python Software Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation.
The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program starts with the outside providers that operators of every size already rely on for advice on which fixes are safe to apply to a running system.
The program is aimed at operational technology in plants, substations and water systems, where equipment built to run for decades often cannot be taken offline for a patch.
Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and to help their customers do the same.
More partners and sectors are due to join over the coming months.
The announcement leaves out the commercial terms.
Axios noted in its coverage that Anthropic has not said whether partners get free model access or who covers the computing costs.
The same report questioned how partners will test and deploy fixes without disrupting utility operations.
Both launches draw on lessons from Project Glasswing.

Reports from the new service go straight to maintainers without human review so they arrive faster.
Some will contain mistakes as a result, such as a wrong severity rating, Anthropic said.
Anthropic expects AI to favor defenders within two years.

extraction.body: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity. The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person. The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January. The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology. “Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.” The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker. Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else. passages: Natura, a relatively unknown hardware startup, has unveiled the Interface - a $99 smart ring that promises to put AI agents on your finger in the most literal sense possible.
Natura's Interface smart ring could mark a turning point for both wearable computing and AI accessibility.

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing.

If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens.
The smart ring market just got its most intriguing entry yet.
Natura is starting with a limited production run of 10,000 units, suggesting either supply constraints or cautious market testing.

"We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions.
The Interface runs on a custom low-power chip that Natura claims delivers up to seven days of battery life - matching or exceeding most competitors.
Instead of positioning itself as a premium lifestyle accessory, Natura is targeting the practical AI user who wants seamless integration without the complexity.
Natura claims its algorithms can detect workout types automatically and provide recovery insights through its companion app.
Industry observers are watching closely to see if Natura can deliver on its ambitious promises.

By combining practical AI agent control with comprehensive health tracking at a breakthrough price point, the device addresses the two biggest barriers facing smart rings: functionality and affordability.

The Interface ring lets users summon AI assistants with a simple press to handle tasks, capture thoughts, and control smart devices - all while tracking health metrics like traditional fitness wearables.

Natura, a relatively unknown hardware startup, has unveiled the Interface - a $99 smart ring that promises to put AI agents on your finger in the most literal sense possible. The device lets users summon AI assistants with simple finger gestures, handling everything from voice memos to smart home control without ever pulling out a phone. While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing. The Interface combines the health monitoring capabilities users expect - heart rate, sleep tracking, activity monitoring - with something entirely new: gesture-controlled AI interaction. "We're not trying to replace your smartphone," the company explains in its launch materials. "We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions. A double-tap might capture a voice memo, while a long press could trigger smart home routines or send pre-programmed messages. The Interface runs on a custom low-power chip that Natura claims delivers up to seven days of battery life - matching or exceeding most competitors. The ring connects via Bluetooth to smartphones and can operate independently for basic functions like health tracking when disconnected. What sets the Interface apart isn't just price, but approach. Instead of positioning itself as a premium lifestyle accessory, Natura is targeting the practical AI user who wants seamless integration without the complexity. The ring works with major AI platforms including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google Assistant, and Amazon Alexa, though users can customize which services respond to specific gestures. The health tracking capabilities appear comprehensive despite the budget positioning. The Interface monitors heart rate variability, sleep stages, blood oxygen levels, and stress indicators - the full suite that's become standard in premium wearables. Natura claims its algorithms can detect workout types automatically and provide recovery insights through its companion app. Industry observers are watching closely to see if Natura can deliver on its ambitious promises. Smart rings have struggled with adoption partly due to high prices and limited functionality beyond health tracking. By adding AI agent control at a fraction of competitor pricing, the Interface could represent the breakthrough the category needs. If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens. The ring format offers something smartphones can't: truly hands-free interaction that doesn't require voice commands or visual attention. Early reviews won't be available until the Interface ships in November, but pre-orders begin next week. Natura is starting with a limited production run of 10,000 units, suggesting either supply constraints or cautious market testing. The company hasn't disclosed funding details, but industry sources suggest significant backing from unnamed Silicon Valley investors. For consumers, the Interface represents a fascinating value proposition: premium smart ring features plus AI agent control for less than the cost of most fitness trackers. Whether Natura can execute on that promise while maintaining build quality and battery life remains the key question facing this ambitious newcomer. Natura's Interface smart ring could mark a turning point for both wearable computing and AI accessibility. By combining practical AI agent control with comprehensive health tracking at a breakthrough price point, the device addresses the two biggest barriers facing smart rings: functionality and affordability. If the execution matches the ambition, we might be looking at the first truly mainstream smart ring - and a preview of how AI integration will evolve beyond our phones and computers into seamlessly integrated everyday objects.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents.
With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone.
And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.
The smart ring was not the company’s first product.
Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price.
For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so.
The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components.

“This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small.
AI and hardware startup Natura has introduced Interface, a $99 smart ring built so people can talk to personal AI agents without digging for a phone.
An always-on agent remote At launch, Interface is designed to work with a range of agents and apps, including Meta's Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude and ChatGPT.

Natura argues that mix of high-quality health sensing, agent communication, meeting recording and "external memory," packed into a small ring with long battery life, sets it apart from health-first rings such as Oura and Ultrahuman and from AI-focused wearables such as Pebble and Vocci.

Price, subscription and timing The launch price is $99, intentionally lower than manufacturing costs Natura compares to Oura and Samsung Galaxy Ring class devices, so the company can get hardware into people's hands and build habits before raising the sticker price later.
From earbuds to a ring Interface is not Natura's first product.

Beyond agents, Ferraris said the ring can also drive phones, computers and other devices — filling forms, messaging, finding files or drafting presentations through spoken requests — and he expects rings to become a primary way people interact with technology as personal agents spread beyond early tech adopters.
Agent replies can arrive through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or Natura's NatureOS app.
After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans a $9 monthly subscription.
Natura is also pointing interested buyers to a waitlist on its site ahead of a live San Francisco presentation planned for November 9.

Users who juggle several assistants can route a request to a specific one — for example asking Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, or Grok Bot to handle another chore — without opening a separate app for each.
Ferraris framed the ring as a way to keep agents reachable around the clock.
Health tracking in the mix Alongside agent control, Interface monitors heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep stages, daily movement, step count and skin temperature over time.
Natura, a relatively unknown hardware startup, has unveiled the Interface - a $99 smart ring that promises to put AI agents on your finger in the most literal sense possible.
Natura's Interface smart ring could mark a turning point for both wearable computing and AI accessibility.

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing.

If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens.

story.title: Natura’s $99 smart ring puts AI agents on your finger

facts.text: Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents.
With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone.
And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.
The smart ring was not the company’s first product.
Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price.
For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so.
The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components.

“This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small.
AI and hardware startup Natura has introduced Interface, a $99 smart ring built so people can talk to personal AI agents without digging for a phone.
An always-on agent remote At launch, Interface is designed to work with a range of agents and apps, including Meta's Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude and ChatGPT.

Natura argues that mix of high-quality health sensing, agent communication, meeting recording and "external memory," packed into a small ring with long battery life, sets it apart from health-first rings such as Oura and Ultrahuman and from AI-focused wearables such as Pebble and Vocci.

Price, subscription and timing The launch price is $99, intentionally lower than manufacturing costs Natura compares to Oura and Samsung Galaxy Ring class devices, so the company can get hardware into people's hands and build habits before raising the sticker price later.
From earbuds to a ring Interface is not Natura's first product.

Beyond agents, Ferraris said the ring can also drive phones, computers and other devices — filling forms, messaging, finding files or drafting presentations through spoken requests — and he expects rings to become a primary way people interact with technology as personal agents spread beyond early tech adopters.
Agent replies can arrive through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or Natura's NatureOS app.
After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans a $9 monthly subscription.
Natura is also pointing interested buyers to a waitlist on its site ahead of a live San Francisco presentation planned for November 9.

Users who juggle several assistants can route a request to a specific one — for example asking Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, or Grok Bot to handle another chore — without opening a separate app for each.
Ferraris framed the ring as a way to keep agents reachable around the clock.
Health tracking in the mix Alongside agent control, Interface monitors heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep stages, daily movement, step count and skin temperature over time.

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. President Donald Trump on Thursday opened up a new front in his ongoing war against commonly used terms and geographic names by warning that anyone referring to Large Language Models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude as “Artificial Intelligence” would earn themselves a place on his enemies list. Writing on Truth Social, he declared that the White House “considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” The president’s outburst-cum-veiled threat landed just over a week after he signed an executive order directing executive branch agencies to begin referring to artificial intelligence, which is now embedded across the federal government, as “super intelligence” following a lunch with leaders in the AI industry, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Dario Amodei and others. That widely mocked directive followed bizarre remarks to the U.N. General Assembly in which he declared that the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” for regulating AI and declaring that the technology would be “hereinafter officially called super intelligence” because “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake.” “It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing,” said Trump, who the week before had launched a poll in his Truth Social feed over the weekend asking respondents to vote for either “Super Intelligence,” “Superior Intelligence,” or “Extreme Intelligence.” The president’s latest linguistic ultimatum is the most recent example of his ongoing effort to change the minds of voters — including many of his own supporters — who’ve increasingly soured on the industry that has tied itself tightly to his unpopular administration. In recent months, that souring has shown up in nearly every poll that asks about AI. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters taken late last month found 73 percent oppose "the building of an AI data center in your community," including 55 percent of Republicans, and 79 percent said safety matters more than keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development. Just 25 percent approve of Trump's handling of the technology against 58 percent who disapprove, and 71 percent said they'd be more likely to back a candidate who supports "stricter guardrails" on it — a figure that includes a majority of Republicans, at 52 percent, and nearly three-quarters of independents. A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September put overall opinion of AI at 37 percent favorable to 60 percent unfavorable, a net rating of minus 23 that has worsened from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle data centers by 14 points, and that among those who oppose the facilities anywhere, Democrats lead the generic ballot by at least 19 points. Trump’s demand for widespread adoption of “super intelligence” in lieu of AI comes just over a month after his last attempt at linguistic coercion, an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The order to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border came in a fit of rage over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa and echoed a similar move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” While the president does have the authority to direct how the government recognizes the names of places and landmarks, he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions. The same goes for use of the term “super intelligence.” He can direct the government to use it but he cannot force Americans — or anyone else — to use his preferred terminology. The Independent has reached out to NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic regarding whether the companies have any plans to use the president’s new terminology in promotional materials or other customer communications; none responded. But the White House has touted a short list of tech CEOs who’d used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang. Complicating the matter, the word superintelligence already means an AI system that surpasses human intellect and ability across multiple domains in couding reasoning, social skills and scientific research — a step toward the kind of rogue AI that many fear, sparking the calls for guardrails and kill switches. President Donald Trump on Thursday opened up a new front in his ongoing war against commonly used terms and geographic names by warning that anyone referring to Large Language Models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude as “Artificial Intelligence” would earn themselves a place on his enemies list.

Writing on Truth Social, he declared that the White House “considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!”

The president’s outburst-cum-veiled threat landed just over a week after he signed an executive order directing executive branch agencies to begin referring to artificial intelligence, which is now embedded across the federal government, as “super intelligence” following a lunch with leaders in the AI industry, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Dario Amodei and others.

That widely mocked directive followed bizarre remarks to the U.N. General Assembly in which he declared that the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” for regulating AI and declaring that the technology would be “hereinafter officially called super intelligence” because “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake.”

“It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing,” said Trump, who the week before had launched a poll in his Truth Social feed over the weekend asking respondents to vote for either “Super Intelligence,” “Superior Intelligence,” or “Extreme Intelligence.”

The president’s latest linguistic ultimatum is the most recent example of his ongoing effort to change the minds of voters — including many of his own supporters — who’ve increasingly soured on the industry that has tied itself tightly to his unpopular administration.

In recent months, that souring has shown up in nearly every poll that asks about AI. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters taken late last month found 73 percent oppose "the building of an AI data center in your community," including 55 percent of Republicans, and 79 percent said safety matters more than keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development.

Just 25 percent approve of Trump's handling of the technology against 58 percent who disapprove, and 71 percent said they'd be more likely to back a candidate who supports "stricter guardrails" on it — a figure that includes a majority of Republicans, at 52 percent, and nearly three-quarters of independents.

A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September put overall opinion of AI at 37 percent favorable to 60 percent unfavorable, a net rating of minus 23 that has worsened from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle data centers by 14 points, and that among those who oppose the facilities anywhere, Democrats lead the generic ballot by at least 19 points.

Trump’s demand for widespread adoption of “super intelligence” in lieu of AI comes just over a month after his last attempt at linguistic coercion, an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

The order to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border came in a fit of rage over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa and echoed a similar move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

While the president does have the authority to direct how the government recognizes the names of places and landmarks, he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions.
The same goes for use of the term “super intelligence.” He can direct the government to use it but he cannot force Americans — or anyone else — to use his preferred terminology.

The Independent has reached out to NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic regarding whether the companies have any plans to use the president’s new terminology in promotional materials or other customer communications; none responded.
But the White House has touted a short list of tech CEOs who’d used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang.

Complicating the matter, the word superintelligence already means an AI system that surpasses human intellect and ability across multiple domains in couding reasoning, social skills and scientific research — a step toward the kind of rogue AI that many fear, sparking the calls for guardrails and kill switches.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has warned people against using the term “artificial intelligence”, saying those who ignore his preferred phrase, “super intelligence”, will be considered “THE ENEMY”. Trump made the remarks in a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. He did not specify what action or consequences would follow for those who continue to use the term “artificial intelligence”. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Trump wrote. Trump Pushes For ‘Super Intelligence’ Trump first proposed replacing “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly last month. At the time, he said the new term “sounds much better”. In late September, Trump also signed an executive order requiring the use of the term “super intelligence” across the US government. The order, however, does not apply to private companies. Despite this, some businesses and technology figures have already started using the term. Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, has adopted the phrase, while Trump ally Elon Musk has also used “super intelligence” in posts on his social media platform X. Political Debate Over AI Terminology The debate over the terminology comes amid growing concerns about artificial intelligence, including questions around its safety and the rapid expansion of data centres across the US. Trump has strongly supported the development of AI but has also sought to present the technology in a more positive light as concerns over its risks continue to grow. The president has also previously pushed for changes to the names of places. He now refers to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” and has called Lake Ontario “Lake America”.

General Assembly in which he declared that the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” for regulating AI and declaring that the technology would be “hereinafter officially called super intelligence” because “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake.”

The president’s latest linguistic ultimatum is the most recent example of his ongoing effort to change the minds of voters — including many of his own supporters — who’ve increasingly soured on the industry that has tied itself tightly to his unpopular administration.

In recent months, that souring has shown up in nearly every poll that asks about AI. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters taken late last month found 73 percent oppose "the building of an AI data center in your community," including 55 percent of Republicans, and 79 percent said safety matters more than keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development.

Trump made the remarks in a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. He did not specify what action or consequences would follow for those who continue to use the term “artificial intelligence”. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Trump wrote. Trump Pushes For ‘Super Intelligence’ Trump first proposed replacing “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly last month. At the time, he said the new term “sounds much better”. In late September, Trump also signed an executive order requiring the use of the term “super intelligence” across the US government. The order, however, does not apply to private companies. Despite this, some businesses and technology figures have already started using the term. Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, has adopted the phrase, while Trump ally Elon Musk has also used “super intelligence” in posts on his social media platform X. Political Debate Over AI Terminology The debate over the terminology comes amid growing concerns about artificial intelligence, including questions around its safety and the rapid expansion of data centres across the US. Trump has strongly supported the development of AI but has also sought to present the technology in a more positive light as concerns over its risks continue to grow. The president has also previously pushed for changes to the names of places. He now refers to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” and has called Lake Ontario “Lake America”.

Hamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s.
“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M.
Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper.
“Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers.
Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck.
“She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.”
During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time.

A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.”

Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming.
