extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep. 30. She was 90. A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO. Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.” “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.” Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree. Hamilton soon found a temporary position in the meteorology department at MIT, working with professor of meteorology Edward N. Lorenz SM ’43, ScD ’48 on weather prediction software. This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory. From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time. In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project. Hamilton worked first on the software for the uncrewed Apollo missions and then was promoted into leading the team developing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions. By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software. “From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 . “There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s. Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” “Defensive” programming and priority-driven software take humans to the moon Hamilton discovered a talent for leadership, as well as a keen instinct for problem-solving and critical thinking that would prove to save Project Apollo several times over. There was the incident that became known as “the Lauren error”: One day, her daughter Lauren, then four years old, was playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab when she somehow activated a pre-launch program, called P01, while the simulator was in midflight — which crashed the simulator altogether. Hamilton created a program add-on in the technical documentation warning users not to launch P01 during flight. She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake. Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish. Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program. This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton’s most famous contribution to the Apollo program came during the pivotal Apollo 11 mission to land on the moon in July of 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm. It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure. But Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software, able to shut down unnecessary background tasks in order to prioritize mission-critical tasks. Houston trusted Hamilton’s software and allowed the mission to proceed, and two men walked on the moon for the first time. Hamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the Instrumentation Lab spun out of MIT to become the independent Draper Laboratory . “Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M. Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.” Hamilton went on to create her first software company, Higher Order Software, in 1976. The firm was based on Hamilton’s software engineering approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.” Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming. Throughout her career, Hamilton worked to achieve recognition for software engineering as a dedicated discipline. “I fought to bring the software legitimacy so that it — and those building it — would be given its due respect, and thus I began to use the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other kinds of engineering, yet treat each type of engineering as part of the overall systems engineering process,” Hamilton told El Pais in 2018 . “When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing. It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline.” Among her many awards and honors, Hamilton was recognized with the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for scientific and technical contributions in 2003; the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017; the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019; and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online. In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub. And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide. “Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck. “She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.” Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. A memorial service will take place in the spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics.

“The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.”

Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree.

This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory.

From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time.

In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project.

Hamilton worked first on the software for the uncrewed Apollo missions and then was promoted into leading the team developing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions. By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software.

“From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 . “There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s. Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”

Hamilton discovered a talent for leadership, as well as a keen instinct for problem-solving and critical thinking that would prove to save Project Apollo several times over.

There was the incident that became known as “the Lauren error”: One day, her daughter Lauren, then four years old, was playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab when she somehow activated a pre-launch program, called P01, while the simulator was in midflight — which crashed the simulator altogether. Hamilton created a program add-on in the technical documentation warning users not to launch P01 during flight.

She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake. Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish. Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program. This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.

Hamilton’s most famous contribution to the Apollo program came during the pivotal Apollo 11 mission to land on the moon in July of 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm. It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure.

But Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software, able to shut down unnecessary background tasks in order to prioritize mission-critical tasks. Houston trusted Hamilton’s software and allowed the mission to proceed, and two men walked on the moon for the first time.
Hamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the Instrumentation Lab spun out of MIT to become the independent Draper Laboratory .

“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M. Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.”
Hamilton went on to create her first software company, Higher Order Software, in 1976. The firm was based on Hamilton’s software engineering approach of error prevention and fault tolerance.

A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.”

Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming.
Throughout her career, Hamilton worked to achieve recognition for software engineering as a dedicated discipline.

“I fought to bring the software legitimacy so that it — and those building it — would be given its due respect, and thus I began to use the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other kinds of engineering, yet treat each type of engineering as part of the overall systems engineering process,” Hamilton told El Pais in 2018 . “When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing. It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline.”

Among her many awards and honors, Hamilton was recognized with the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for scientific and technical contributions in 2003; the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017; the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019; and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022.

Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online. In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub. And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide.

“Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck. “She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.”

Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. A memorial service will take place in the spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.

Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

“She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

MIT News also said Hamilton worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and later founded two software companies, and ABC News said she was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, including through a Lego set unveiled in 2017 that included a figure of Hamilton.
Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement.
She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.”
Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project.

She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake.
Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program.
This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.
Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm.
It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure.
A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline.

Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online.
In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub.

And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide.
By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software.

“From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 .

Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project.

She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake.
Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program.
This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.
Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm.

A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline.

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep. 30. She was 90. A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO. Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.” “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.” Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree. Hamilton soon found a temporary position in the meteorology department at MIT, working with professor of meteorology Edward N. Lorenz SM ’43, ScD ’48 on weather prediction software. This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory. From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time. In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project. Hamilton worked first on the software for the uncrewed Apollo missions and then was promoted into leading the team developing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions. A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO.

Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.”

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics.

“The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.”

Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree.

Hamilton soon found a temporary position in the meteorology department at MIT, working with professor of meteorology Edward N. Lorenz SM ’43, ScD ’48 on weather prediction software. This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory.

From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time.

In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. extraction.body: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that anyone who doesn't use his preferred term of super intelligence (SI) will be considered an "enemy" of the White House. "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump's statement suggests the White House may punish companies or individuals who do not abide by its preferred speech, which would be a potential textbook First Amendment violation if enforced. The White House has moved to rebrand artificial intelligence, which Trump said suggests that the technology is "fake." While some companies, most notably Meta, which has a SuperIntelligence Labs, had super intelligence embedded in their branding before Trump's recent move, their descriptions were more about the future of artificial intelligence than an outright rejection of the terminology itself. After meeting with industry leaders in late September at the White House, Trump signed an executive order that required federal departments and agencies "to the maximum extent permitted by law" to use "'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites," among other official communications. The order did not apply to private-sector companies like OpenAI because the White House has no legal authority to enforce such a measure. Since Trump's statements and orders, at least one company has followed the White House's wishes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the space and technology company would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI. If Musk follows through on his promise, it would be the second such rebrand for what was originally known as xAI this year. In February, SpaceX announced that it was acquiring xAI, makers of the Grok chatbot, and rechristened the unit as SpaceXAI in July. As of Thursday afternoon, SpaceXAI's X account still said "SpaceXAI." It remains to be seen what other leading AI and tech companies will do. There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch. During a White House panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Wang corrected himself when he said "AI" instead of "SI." In comments made with Trump standing just feet from him, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the company "builds artificial intelligence" to help everyone. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently dismissed the possibility of renaming the company during an interview with Politico. "No plans to do that," he told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot and we will continue to talk about it."

facts.text: Well then... perhaps Donald Trump will understand how 10's of millions of Americans feel as they deem him, and his supporters, ,"the enemy" and target him, as well as his supporters, with their ballots as voting in the midterm elections begins.
On October 8, Marjorie Taylor Greene took aim at Trump after he said those using the term ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and not ‘Super Intelligence’ will be considered enemies.
Earlier in the day, the POTUS shared the post saying:
“As Americans struggle to afford groceries, rent, and gas … the President is spending his time worried about branding.
TRUMP is out of touch, and people are paying the price for his aloofness!”
Jim McGovern also gave his reaction to the president’s post on Artificial Intelligence, saying:
He stated that the reason behind the new name was that ‘artificial’ made it appear ‘fake’; so he decided to use the word ‘super.’
Besides, the POTUS signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence with tech leaders like Elon Musk and Dario Amodei .

"The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social.
There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that anyone who doesn't use his preferred term of super intelligence (SI) will be considered an "enemy" of the White House. "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump's statement suggests the White House may punish companies or individuals who do not abide by its preferred speech, which would be a potential textbook First Amendment violation if enforced. The White House has moved to rebrand artificial intelligence, which Trump said suggests that the technology is "fake." While some companies, most notably Meta, which has a SuperIntelligence Labs, had super intelligence embedded in their branding before Trump's recent move, their descriptions were more about the future of artificial intelligence than an outright rejection of the terminology itself. After meeting with industry leaders in late September at the White House, Trump signed an executive order that required federal departments and agencies "to the maximum extent permitted by law" to use "'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites," among other official communications. The order did not apply to private-sector companies like OpenAI because the White House has no legal authority to enforce such a measure. Since Trump's statements and orders, at least one company has followed the White House's wishes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the space and technology company would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI. If Musk follows through on his promise, it would be the second such rebrand for what was originally known as xAI this year. In February, SpaceX announced that it was acquiring xAI, makers of the Grok chatbot, and rechristened the unit as SpaceXAI in July. As of Thursday afternoon, SpaceXAI's X account still said "SpaceXAI." It remains to be seen what other leading AI and tech companies will do. There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch. During a White House panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Wang corrected himself when he said "AI" instead of "SI." In comments made with Trump standing just feet from him, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the company "builds artificial intelligence" to help everyone. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently dismissed the possibility of renaming the company during an interview with Politico. "No plans to do that," he told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot and we will continue to talk about it."

passages: Washington [US], October 8 (ANI): US President Donald Trump will present the nation's highest honours for scientific and technological achievement to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other leading American innovators on Thursday (local time), marking the first time he will present the awards during either of his administrations, Fox News reported.Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, while Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, according to Fox News Digital.Musk's expected award also marks another step in his renewed relationship with Trump following a high-profile rupture between the two last year.

Musk recently appeared alongside Trump at a lunch with technology leaders and was also present during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, according to Fox News.The recipients will be recognised at the White House's "Science: A New Golden Age Summit", which will bring together leading scientists and technology innovators to discuss how superintelligence and private-sector investment can accelerate scientific breakthroughs and strengthen US leadership in science and technology."The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology.
The split followed Musk's departure from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), after which he criticised Trump's signature tax-and-spending legislation as a "disgusting abomination".
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

extraction.body: Washington [US], October 8 (ANI): US President Donald Trump will present the nation's highest honours for scientific and technological achievement to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other leading American innovators on Thursday (local time), marking the first time he will present the awards during either of his administrations, Fox News reported.Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, while Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, according to Fox News Digital.Musk's expected award also marks another step in his renewed relationship with Trump following a high-profile rupture between the two last year. The split followed Musk's departure from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), after which he criticised Trump's signature tax-and-spending legislation as a "disgusting abomination". The dispute escalated into a public feud, with Trump threatening Musk's government contracts, Fox News reported.Trump and Musk have since renewed their ties. Musk recently appeared alongside Trump at a lunch with technology leaders and was also present during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, according to Fox News.The recipients will be recognised at the White House's "Science: A New Golden Age Summit", which will bring together leading scientists and technology innovators to discuss how superintelligence and private-sector investment can accelerate scientific breakthroughs and strengthen US leadership in science and technology."The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology. These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation," White House spokesperson Liz Huston told Fox News Digital.The ceremony will mark Trump's first time presenting both the National Medal of Science and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation during either of his presidential administrations.The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has also returned to an advisory role in the Trump administration, co-leading the Pentagon's Project Meridian, which studies the future of warfare and the weapons and technologies the US military will need to maintain its technological edge.The award also has a personal connection for Trump. His uncle, John G Trump, was posthumously awarded the National Medal of Science by then-President Ronald Reagan for his pioneering work involving ionising radiation and its applications in medicine, industry and atomic physics.The White House summit is expected to focus on the role of scientific innovation, emerging technologies and private-sector investment in advancing research and maintaining US leadership in science and technology, Fox News reported.The National Medal of Science was established by the US Congress in 1959 and is the highest recognition the nation can bestow on scientists and engineers.According to the National Medal of Science, the presidential award is given to individuals for outstanding contributions to knowledge in the physical, biological, mathematical, engineering, or social and behavioural sciences in service to the nation. The broad areas covered by the award include disciplines such as astronomy, chemistry, computer and information science and engineering, geoscience, materials research and STEM education.A committee of distinguished scientists and engineers appointed by the US President evaluates nominees for the award, which is presented by the President at a White House ceremony.Since its establishment, the National Medal of Science has been awarded to 529 distinguished scientists and engineers whose careers span decades of research and development. (ANI)(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

The president was speaking at the New Golden Age Summit at the Institute of Peace in Washington, where his administration introduced over $6 billion in investments to incubate scientific discovery. "From day one, my administration has taken decisive action to ensure that America continues to dominate the frontiers of science and technology," the president said before handing out the awards. "Today, it is my privilege to bestow National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation on some of those very same technology leaders — people whose contributions to their fields will be remembered in the annals of science forever." Elon Musk was the first to receive an award. The tech billionaire who founded and currently runs SpaceX, Tesla, Neuralink and xAI — and who spent at least $230 million of his own money to help elect Trump in 2024 — received the National Medal of Science. Trump said Musk is "an industrial titan, a brilliant engineer and one of the greatest technology founders to ever live" whose "genius and determination have made science fiction into reality." Musk later wrote on X: "Thank you on behalf of the amazing people of SpaceX, Tesla, Neuralink and Boring Company, without whom anything I have done would have been possible." Sergey Brin (who co-founded Google), Lisa Su (who is chief executive of Advanced Micro Devices) and Jensen Huang (who co-founded Nvidia) also received the National Medal of Science — the highest honor the president can bestow on a scientist or engineer who has made outstanding contributions in the fields of physical, biological, mathematical, engineering or social and behavioral sciences. Michael Dell, who dropped out of the University of Texas at age 19 to launch an eponymous computer business that would grow into one of the world's most valuable companies, and Satya Nadella, who runs Microsoft, were each awarded with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation — the highest honor the president can bestow for technological achievement. Trump handed out the awards the same day his administration announced it is suspending Microsoft from an employment-based green card program for foreign workers, alleging the company fraudulently uses the H-1B visa program to discriminate against Americans. On Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general announced it is investigating J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities it alleges have improperly used the visa classification to avoid employment obligations, exploit taxpayer funding and undermine American workers. Stanford University, attended by half of Thursday's national medal recipients, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, attended by one of the national medal recipients, are among the schools that are being investigated. The awards were handed out one day after the Department of Homeland Security proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States as part of a broader Trump administration crackdown on legal immigration and foreign visa programs. Five out of the six national medal recipients were born outside the United States. "We live in an age of American wonders and technological marvels, and with the help of the brilliant men and women here today, we will always be on top," Trump said. "There's nobody that can compete with us. Nobody." Among the investments the White House announced at the summit are $2.4 billion in contributions from Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI and other companies to provide compute credits for scientists, and $1 billion from universities, industry and the state of Georgia for scientific computing and related workforce training efforts for students, according to a White House fact sheet.

coreStoryFacts.text: Washington [US], October 8 (ANI): US President Donald Trump will present the nation's highest honours for scientific and technological achievement to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other leading American innovators on Thursday (local time), marking the first time he will present the awards during either of his administrations, Fox News reported.Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, while Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, according to Fox News Digital.Musk's expected award also marks another step in his renewed relationship with Trump following a high-profile rupture between the two last year.

Musk recently appeared alongside Trump at a lunch with technology leaders and was also present during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, according to Fox News.The recipients will be recognised at the White House's "Science: A New Golden Age Summit", which will bring together leading scientists and technology innovators to discuss how superintelligence and private-sector investment can accelerate scientific breakthroughs and strengthen US leadership in science and technology."The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology.
The split followed Musk's departure from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), after which he criticised Trump's signature tax-and-spending legislation as a "disgusting abomination".

relevantPassages.text: Washington [US], October 8 (ANI): US President Donald Trump will present the nation's highest honours for scientific and technological achievement to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other leading American innovators on Thursday (local time), marking the first time he will present the awards during either of his administrations, Fox News reported.Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, while Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, according to Fox News Digital.Musk's expected award also marks another step in his renewed relationship with Trump following a high-profile rupture between the two last year.

Musk recently appeared alongside Trump at a lunch with technology leaders and was also present during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, according to Fox News.The recipients will be recognised at the White House's "Science: A New Golden Age Summit", which will bring together leading scientists and technology innovators to discuss how superintelligence and private-sector investment can accelerate scientific breakthroughs and strengthen US leadership in science and technology."The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology.
The split followed Musk's departure from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), after which he criticised Trump's signature tax-and-spending legislation as a "disgusting abomination".

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump awarded national medals for science, technology and innovation on Thursday to the leaders and founders of six American companies he said are "helping pioneer an incredible future." The president was speaking at the New Golden Age Summit at the Institute of Peace in Washington, where his administration introduced over $6 billion in investments to incubate scientific discovery. "From day one, my administration has taken decisive action to ensure that America continues to dominate the frontiers of science and technology," the president said before handing out the awards. "Today, it is my privilege to bestow National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation on some of those very same technology leaders — people whose contributions to their fields will be remembered in the annals of science forever." Elon Musk was the first to receive an award. The tech billionaire who founded and currently runs SpaceX, Tesla, Neuralink and xAI — and who spent at least $230 million of his own money to help elect Trump in 2024 — received the National Medal of Science. Trump said Musk is "an industrial titan, a brilliant engineer and one of the greatest technology founders to ever live" whose "genius and determination have made science fiction into reality." Musk later wrote on X: "Thank you on behalf of the amazing people of SpaceX, Tesla, Neuralink and Boring Company, without whom anything I have done would have been possible." Sergey Brin (who co-founded Google), Lisa Su (who is chief executive of Advanced Micro Devices) and Jensen Huang (who co-founded Nvidia) also received the National Medal of Science — the highest honor the president can bestow on a scientist or engineer who has made outstanding contributions in the fields of physical, biological, mathematical, engineering or social and behavioral sciences. Michael Dell, who dropped out of the University of Texas at age 19 to launch an eponymous computer business that would grow into one of the world's most valuable companies, and Satya Nadella, who runs Microsoft, were each awarded with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation — the highest honor the president can bestow for technological achievement. Trump handed out the awards the same day his administration announced it is suspending Microsoft from an employment-based green card program for foreign workers, alleging the company fraudulently uses the H-1B visa program to discriminate against Americans. On Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general announced it is investigating J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities it alleges have improperly used the visa classification to avoid employment obligations, exploit taxpayer funding and undermine American workers. Stanford University, attended by half of Thursday's national medal recipients, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, attended by one of the national medal recipients, are among the schools that are being investigated. The awards were handed out one day after the Department of Homeland Security proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States as part of a broader Trump administration crackdown on legal immigration and foreign visa programs. Five out of the six national medal recipients were born outside the United States. "We live in an age of American wonders and technological marvels, and with the help of the brilliant men and women here today, we will always be on top," Trump said. "There's nobody that can compete with us. Nobody." Among the investments the White House announced at the summit are $2.4 billion in contributions from Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI and other companies to provide compute credits for scientists, and $1 billion from universities, industry and the state of Georgia for scientific computing and related workforce training efforts for students, according to a White House fact sheet.

sources.title: U.S. government moves $1 billion in bitcoin from Bitfinex hack wallet, no sale indicated - Cryptonews.net
passages: Wallets linked to the U.S. government moved 12,267 bitcoin $BTC $81,274.45 , worth about $1.01 billion, on Thursday, according to data provided by blockchain intelligence firm Arkham.
The coins left a wallet holding funds seized in the 2016 Bitfinex hack and went to a new, unlabeled address, with a second transaction going to a different address.
No exchange deposit was recorded, a pattern more consistent with wallet reshuffling than a sale.
The government still holds about $25.5 billion worth of crypto, Arkham shows.
The transfer follows heavier exchange-bound activity 24 hours earlier, when roughly 3,200 $BTC (about $264 million) and $119 million in USDT landed at Coinbase Prime deposit addresses.

extraction.body: Wallets linked to the U.S. government moved 12,267 bitcoin $BTC $81,274.45 , worth about $1.01 billion, on Thursday, according to data provided by blockchain intelligence firm Arkham. The coins left a wallet holding funds seized in the 2016 Bitfinex hack and went to a new, unlabeled address, with a second transaction going to a different address. No exchange deposit was recorded, a pattern more consistent with wallet reshuffling than a sale. The transfer follows heavier exchange-bound activity 24 hours earlier, when roughly 3,200 $BTC (about $264 million) and $119 million in USDT landed at Coinbase Prime deposit addresses. The funds came from wallets tied to the FTX/Alameda and Bitfinex seizures, according to Arkham’s identification. CoinDesk reported on Wednesday that more than $100 million in $BTC and BNB moved in a similar fashion. In July, about $288 million in seized bitcoin and ether was routed to Coinbase Prime via fresh intermediary wallets. Deposits to Coinbase Prime don't necessarily indicate a sale because the platform also provides custody. A March 2025 executive order directed forfeited bitcoin into a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and said it should not be sold. The government still holds about $25.5 billion worth of crypto, Arkham shows. The transfer follows heavier exchange-bound activity 24 hours earlier, when roughly 3,200 BTC (about $264 million) and $119 million in USDT were deposited into Coinbase Prime addresses. The funds came from wallets tied to the FTX/Alameda and Bitfinex seizures, according to Arkham’s identification.

CoinDesk reported on Wednesday that more than $100 million in BTC and BNB moved in a similar fashion. In July, about $288 million in seized bitcoin and ether was routed to Coinbase Prime via fresh intermediary wallets.

Deposits to Coinbase Prime don't necessarily indicate a sale, as the platform also provides custody services. A March 2025 executive order directed that forfeited bitcoin be placed into a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and said it should not be sold. The government still holds about $25.5 billion worth of crypto, Arkham shows.

extraction.body: The European country had no legal framework for taxing crypto — until now. Greece is planning a law to tax crypto investors’ capital gains at a rate of 15%, according to reports. According to Reuters and local media , the country’s Finance Ministry has drafted a bill with the proposal. Greece currently has no legal framework for taxing crypto. Under the draft, the first €500 (about $580) of crypto gains each year would be exempt. The bill would tax only the net gain when crypto is sold, after deducting trading fees. Swapping one cryptocurrency for another, such as bitcoin, would not trigger the tax. It would apply only when holdings are converted into euros or another fiat currency, or used to pay for goods and services. Investors could carry losses forward against future crypto gains for up to five tax years, and tokens earned through staking or lending would be taxed only when sold. The rules would apply retroactively from January 1, 2025, meaning gains from last year onward would be declared on tax returns filed in 2027. The bill is due to be submitted to parliament in November. Greece follows the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation. The Hellenic Capital Market Commission authorizes and supervises crypto service providers, and the Bank of Greece handles prudential oversight of stablecoin issuers. Licensing has been slow: no Greek providers appeared on the EU’s register until September, about two months after MiCA’s transitional period ended on July 1. Since January 2026, the EU’s DAC8 directive has required crypto exchanges to collect detailed data on their users and transactions and report it to national tax authorities, much like banks already do for ordinary accounts. Greece wrote those rules into national law in May. Crypto tax treatment varies widely across the bloc. Rates range from 8% in Cyprus to 30% in France. Some countries are more lenient: Germany exempts crypto held for more than a year, and Portugal does the same after 365 days. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. extraction.body: The European country had no legal framework for taxing crypto — until now. Greece is planning a law to tax crypto investors’ capital gains at a rate of 15%, according to reports. According to Reuters and local media , the country’s Finance Ministry has drafted a bill with the proposal. Greece currently has no legal framework for taxing crypto. Under the draft, the first €500 (about $580) of crypto gains each year would be exempt. The bill would tax only the net gain when crypto is sold, after deducting trading fees. Swapping one cryptocurrency for another, such as bitcoin, would not trigger the tax. It would apply only when holdings are converted into euros or another fiat currency, or used to pay for goods and services. Investors could carry losses forward against future crypto gains for up to five tax years, and tokens earned through staking or lending would be taxed only when sold. The rules would apply retroactively from January 1, 2025, meaning gains from last year onward would be declared on tax returns filed in 2027. The bill is due to be submitted to parliament in November. Greece follows the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation. The Hellenic Capital Market Commission authorizes and supervises crypto service providers, and the Bank of Greece handles prudential oversight of stablecoin issuers. Licensing has been slow: no Greek providers appeared on the EU’s register until September, about two months after MiCA’s transitional period ended on July 1. Since January 2026, the EU’s DAC8 directive has required crypto exchanges to collect detailed data on their users and transactions and report it to national tax authorities, much like banks already do for ordinary accounts. Greece wrote those rules into national law in May. Crypto tax treatment varies widely across the bloc. Rates range from 8% in Cyprus to 30% in France. Some countries are more lenient: Germany exempts crypto held for more than a year, and Portugal does the same after 365 days. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. Since January 2026, the EU’s DAC8 directive has required crypto exchanges to collect detailed data on their users and transactions and report it to national tax authorities, much like banks already do for ordinary accounts. Greece wrote those rules into national law in May.

Crypto tax treatment varies widely across the bloc. Rates range from 8% in Cyprus to 30% in France. Some countries are more lenient: Germany exempts crypto held for more than a year, and Portugal does the same after 365 days.

extraction.body: Bitwise, the world’s largest crypto index fund manager, recently released a report indicating an unwavering commitment among institutional investors toward digital assets. The company’s three-month study, which involved top officials from the world’s largest financial institutions, showed their strategy amid the massive drawdowns in cryptocurrency prices between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026. According to Bitwise, it interviewed “senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions” at 15 of the world’s largest institutions. These included public companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, foundations, public pension funds, investment consultants, and multi-family offices. The respondents revealed that none of them reduced their crypto allocation between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. It came despite a roughly 50% drawdown in Bitcoin (BTC) and correlated altcoins during the period, driven by aggressive US trade policies, geopolitical tensions, rapidly rising inflation, and dramatic accrual of US debt. In fact, some of them even increased their crypto exposure. Interestingly, Bitwise found that all the institutions it covered held Bitcoin. Almost all of them either solely maintained BTC or had their largest exposure in the asset. Additionally, nearly all disclosed that Bitcoin is their longest-held position. Then, most paired BTC with gold, suggesting they treat the premier crypto asset as a digital hedge against macro debasement akin to the precious metal. Bitwise highlighted that their BTC allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets. However, most kept exposure between 1% and 2%. The asset manager noted that allocation size was inversely correlated with the number of people who must approve it. Family offices emerged as the entities with the highest allocations, while sovereign wealth funds had the lowest. Interestingly, respondents couldn’t name a specific price range at which they would be willing to sell their crypto holdings. Nonetheless, they cited thesis failure, regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis as reasons they might abandon their bet on digital assets. What’s more, several institutions held Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL), but only in limited positions and for shorter durations. They are also tied to value accrual rather than serving as a hedge like Bitcoin and gold. Bitwise said the survey results bust the myth that institutions tend to sell during major crypto drawdowns. The report indicates the opposite. Giancarlo is an economist by profession with a career spanning nearly two decades. Prior to his addition to Blockzeit’s dynamic team, he held an essential role as Project Manager for initiatives encompassing blockchain, tokenization, stablecoin, mining, special economic zone development, and iGaming. extraction.body: Bitwise, the world’s largest crypto index fund manager, recently released a report indicating an unwavering commitment among institutional investors toward digital assets. The company’s three-month study, which involved top officials from the world’s largest financial institutions, showed their strategy amid the massive drawdowns in cryptocurrency prices between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026. According to Bitwise, it interviewed “senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions” at 15 of the world’s largest institutions. These included public companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, foundations, public pension funds, investment consultants, and multi-family offices. The respondents revealed that none of them reduced their crypto allocation between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. It came despite a roughly 50% drawdown in Bitcoin (BTC) and correlated altcoins during the period, driven by aggressive US trade policies, geopolitical tensions, rapidly rising inflation, and dramatic accrual of US debt. In fact, some of them even increased their crypto exposure. Interestingly, Bitwise found that all the institutions it covered held Bitcoin. Almost all of them either solely maintained BTC or had their largest exposure in the asset. Additionally, nearly all disclosed that Bitcoin is their longest-held position. Then, most paired BTC with gold, suggesting they treat the premier crypto asset as a digital hedge against macro debasement akin to the precious metal. Bitwise highlighted that their BTC allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets. However, most kept exposure between 1% and 2%. The asset manager noted that allocation size was inversely correlated with the number of people who must approve it. Family offices emerged as the entities with the highest allocations, while sovereign wealth funds had the lowest. Interestingly, respondents couldn’t name a specific price range at which they would be willing to sell their crypto holdings. Nonetheless, they cited thesis failure, regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis as reasons they might abandon their bet on digital assets. What’s more, several institutions held Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL), but only in limited positions and for shorter durations. They are also tied to value accrual rather than serving as a hedge like Bitcoin and gold. Bitwise said the survey results bust the myth that institutions tend to sell during major crypto drawdowns. The report indicates the opposite. Giancarlo is an economist by profession with a career spanning nearly two decades. His professional journey has seen him assume vital roles in various government and private organizations such as the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), Megaworld Corporation, and the China Banking Corporation in the Republic of the Philippines. In addition to his civic and corporate pursuits, his forward-thinking approach has led him to manage several prominent websites in the banking and finance sector, notably the Australia-based RateChoice, where he immersed himself in the world of emerging financial technologies and where he found particular interest in Bitcoin all the way back to 2013. Prior to his addition to Blockzeit’s dynamic team, he held an essential role as Project Manager for initiatives encompassing blockchain, tokenization, stablecoin, mining, special economic zone development, and iGaming. This noteworthy chapter in his career unfolded under the auspices of InPlan Consultancy Services, Inc., the think-tank of IMPERO Consortium Management Corporation headquartered in Manila, Philippines, and Tokyo, Japan. passages: Bitwise, the world’s largest crypto index fund manager, recently released a report indicating an unwavering commitment among institutional investors toward digital assets. The company’s three-month study, which involved top officials from the world’s largest financial institutions, showed their strategy amid the massive drawdowns in cryptocurrency prices between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026.

According to Bitwise, it interviewed “senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions” at 15 of the world’s largest institutions. These included public companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, foundations, public pension funds, investment consultants, and multi-family offices.

The respondents revealed that none of them reduced their crypto allocation between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. It came despite a roughly 50% drawdown in Bitcoin (BTC) and correlated altcoins during the period, driven by aggressive US trade policies, geopolitical tensions, rapidly rising inflation, and dramatic accrual of US debt. In fact, some of them even increased their crypto exposure.
Interestingly, Bitwise found that all the institutions it covered held Bitcoin. Almost all of them either solely maintained BTC or had their largest exposure in the asset.

Additionally, nearly all disclosed that Bitcoin is their longest-held position. Then, most paired BTC with gold, suggesting they treat the premier crypto asset as a digital hedge against macro debasement akin to the precious metal.
Bitwise highlighted that their BTC allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets. However, most kept exposure between 1% and 2%.

The asset manager noted that allocation size was inversely correlated with the number of people who must approve it. Family offices emerged as the entities with the highest allocations, while sovereign wealth funds had the lowest.

Interestingly, respondents couldn’t name a specific price range at which they would be willing to sell their crypto holdings. Nonetheless, they cited thesis failure, regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis as reasons they might abandon their bet on digital assets.

What’s more, several institutions held Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL), but only in limited positions and for shorter durations. They are also tied to value accrual rather than serving as a hedge like Bitcoin and gold.
Bitwise said the survey results bust the myth that institutions tend to sell during major crypto drawdowns. The report indicates the opposite.

His professional journey has seen him assume vital roles in various government and private organizations such as the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), Megaworld Corporation, and the China Banking Corporation in the Republic of the Philippines. In addition to his civic and corporate pursuits, his forward-thinking approach has led him to manage several prominent websites in the banking and finance sector, notably the Australia-based RateChoice, where he immersed himself in the world of emerging financial technologies and where he found particular interest in Bitcoin all the way back to 2013. Prior to his addition to Blockzeit’s dynamic team, he held an essential role as Project Manager for initiatives encompassing blockchain, tokenization, stablecoin, mining, special economic zone development, and iGaming. This noteworthy chapter in his career unfolded under the auspices of InPlan Consultancy Services, Inc., the think-tank of IMPERO Consortium Management Corporation headquartered in Manila, Philippines, and Tokyo, Japan. InPlan, led by a distinguished retired Cabinet member of the Philippines, collaborates directly with IMPERO's core management team, contributing to strategic planning and business development endeavors.

passages: Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake urged the blockchain industry to prepare for “bunker mode” by planning a controlled migration of assets to fresh addresses whose public keys have never been exposed.

Drake warned that AI could find a way to break the mathematics protecting bitcoin and ether wallet signatures in the worst case “in months, not years.” Drake said a wallet uses a secret number called a private key to authorize payments, while a related public key lets the network check those approvals, and he argued AI might help someone recover the secret from the public key.
Drake recommended that large and sophisticated holders begin a gradual move first, and he said the process should be calm rather than a stampede to avoid errors and direct losses.

Drake said he would “be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration” on Ethereum’s post-quantum shift, and he argued that exiting bunker mode safely “will require post-AI cryptography.” Drake described his personal preference as going “all-in on hash-based cryptography” and avoiding structured mathematical assumptions from curves, lattices, or isogenies.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin backed Drake’s warning while urging holders not to rush, writing, “I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today.” Buterin said the risk deserves serious attention and added, “But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously.” Buterin extended the concern beyond elliptic curves by warning that lattice-based cryptography could face “serious hits” within the next two years due to AI-driven mathematical advances.
CoinDesk and Cryptonews.net both stress Drake’s bunker-mode call and no demonstrated break yet, with care to avoid rushed migrations.
Drake also said wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from “Satoshi's shield,” and he described “20K exposed addresses” tied to Bitcoin’s creator as holding 50 BTC each.
